he must wait a full year before making application again, and whether his application
should be made by simply presenting himself to the Lodge as an Apprentice or Fellow Craft, well skilled and proficient in all the work a.nd learning of his degree, and
again asking simply to be advanced ; or whether his petition must be presented to the
[,odge in form, and must take the course of other petitions for degrees or member·
ship. In some other jurisdictions where separate ballots are had, only one petition
is presented. If that is favorably received, the applicant is initiated ; and when, in
his own judgment, he has made suitable proficiency, he makes verbal request only
for advancement; and upon that, without reference or delay, the second ballot is had·
If that is unfavorable for any reason, he may apply again at the next or any other
stated meeting of the Lodge, and is not required to wait the time prescribed for those
rejected upon original petition. The rule may be different in other States. i.:nder
our rule, if objection is sustained, the party is still a member of the Lodge of his degree, and entitled to all his privileges as such. In the case presented, I decided that
the objection sustained was in effect a rejection for the remaining degrees; that the
party so rejected must wait twelve months, and then, if be desired to proceed, he
must petition his Lodge anew ; and that his petition must take the usual course. In
any view of the case he was entitled to that, if no more. Yon will determine the
rule by which we shall in future be guided in such cases.
There seems to be some diversity of opinion as to the effect of a rever~al by the
Grand Lodge of a judgment of suspension or expulsion made by one of its suborninatns.
.Among a good many the opinion prevails that if a member is once suspended or ex·
pelled, his membership with the Lodge is forever severe'd, no matter what action the
Grand Lodge may take in the case on appeal. Cases have been brought to my notice where Masters have so held. In all such cases I have instructed tho parties
interested that the reversal by the Grand Lodge of the judgment of a subordinate
Lodge restored the party to all his rights, and left him in precisely the same relations
of membership as before the charges were preferred. I mention the matter here,
not because there is any doubt in my mind as to the effect of such reversal upon the
merits of a case, but to bring the rule in such cases to the attention of the brethren
more conveniently than I could otherwise do.
In this connection I may mention a case which occurred in :Si. John's I,odge, No.
37. Sometime in the latter part of the winter, charges were preferred against
-0ne of its members. He was tried by the commission appointed for the purpose,
adjudged guilty upon one of the specifications, and sentenced to be reprimanded. Within the time allowed for appeals, one of the commissioners who tried
the case filed a notice and perfected an appeal. I,ast month business called me to
Yreka, where the Lodge is held, and while there the c.ase was brought to my atten·
tion. Being of opinion that a member of the Court which sat in judgment was not
one of the parties to whom au appeal was allowed, I directed the acting Master, the
Senior Warden of the Lodge, to carry the sentence into effect at the next stated
meeting. By our Constitution an appeal should, in no case, delay the execution
of a sentence of reprimand; but if it should, it is not doubtful who may appeal. The
language of the Constitution is, " An appeal may be taken to the Grand Lodge by
eUher party;" and, according to the well established legal maxim that the expression of a particular intent excludes every other, no one except the partiestbe accuser or the accused-can appeal. If the law is not comprehensive enough,
Jet us enlarge it to include all who should be included. But, apart from technical oh·
jections, it seemed to me particularly out of character for the Court, or any member
of it to take an appeal from its own judgment.

I have also been asked, in a single instance, whether the applicant must be able
t.o read and write, and whether the fact that he can do neither th~ one nor the other
is sufficient cause for refusing his petition or rejecting the petitioner; and I suggest
the question for your consideration. I do not find it written in the Ancient Charges
or Constitutions that the applicant for the mysteries of Masonry must be able to
1·ead the holy book, or su bscrlbe his name to hls petition with his own hand. In the
"arlier times it is probable that very few of even the worthiest and most distinguished
of the Craft were able to read or write; and we are told on good authority that at
the time the great Charter of English liberty was extorted from King John, not one
of the Barons of England, whose names were aftlxed to that instrument, could write
!tis own name upon it. Books were few and of great cost. Only the favored few
were clerks and scholars. But in this day and in this land, where the facilities for
education are at every man's door, can we say that the applicant who sends us his peti·
Lion, with an X for his signature, is a good and true man-able to do Ills master's
work-however blameless bis character may be1 I think not. He who, in•our day
and in our country, so far forgets himself as to grow up to the stature of a man with·
out being able to read or write, or who, having arrived at man's estate, neglects to,
1<cquire that ability, is not deserving a place in our midst. He is not just and true t<>
himself, nor can he be so to us.
That the ballot should ani must be secret and sacred, is one of the llrst prlnciple11,
we are taught in Maaonry-one without which we could not maintain the purity of
the institution. All authority, ancient and modern, proclaims it a law of Masonry as
lnfiexible as the laws of the Medes and Persians. Our own Constitution provides
U1at, when a ballot bas been had, if but one black ball appear, tlio Master may, to
nvoid a possible error, before declaring the result, order a socoml ballot. ·It would
Huem that a rule so 1il11in could not be mistaken, yet many do mistake it, or, in their
11nxiety for the election of friends, they disregard it. Several instances 11ave been
hl'ought to my notice. In one, tho Master ordered a second and third ballot, when
there were two black balls at each ballot. In another, the first bt1llot resulting un·
favorably, the Master, without declariug the result, postponed a second ballot to the
next stated meceting. In another, the first ballot resulting unfavorably, was de·
dared, and afterwards, at the •ame meeting, one ol' the members ht1ving 1·etlred,
1111other ballot was had by whicl1 the candidate w11.s elected. In another, after ar~
unfavorable ballot the subject wa.~ canvassed, and a member RnMpected of liaving
1'a•t the black ball 'was so hard pressed by the friends of the candidate that he confoHHed the fact, and, in open I,odgt1, declared tlmt ho would continue to do so aK
often as tllc ballot Hlwuld be taken. In anotlrnr, two black balls appearing, the
M11ster submitted tlle qncRtion to his J,ollge, whether a Hecoud ballot should be had!
Oftentimes the candidate Is informed of his rejection and who is suspected of having
c1111sed it, almost as soon a.~ the Lodge iH clonetl. Such things ought not to Ile, and<
11111Ht not be. Every Mnster of a Lodge •hould at least read, and, if need be, study
11111' Constitution and Hegulations; and if' lie sl;ould do so it would seem that he could
11ot avoid learning thel'efrom that, wl1en but one black ball appears, he may order a
•••cond ballot to correct a posHil>le crror--that this is a matter purely of discretion with
hil11, and that, with the second ballot, bis discretion it1 oxlmusted--and that he may

I may be sorry that my friend, whose petition I have taken into the Lodge, is not.
the friend of everybody there ; bnt if he has been rejected, I may very properly
suppose that some one has good cause to reject him. It is essential to our very
existence that the ballot be preserved secret and sacred.
There seems to be a growing disposition on the part of some of our brethren to
take part in public celebrations and festivities, as a distinct body. I can hardly conceive whence this desire comes. Surely, it is not among the lessons we are taught.
in the Lodge, that we should be forward to proclaim to the world-behold we are
Masons !-or anxious or willing to assist at any celebration or ceremony not purely
Masonic in its character. On no occasion, except for the burial of a brother, fa it
permitted for any Lodge or number of Masons to appear in ?tfosonic clothing in public procession, without special permission from the Grand Master; and that permission ought very rarely to be asked or granted. We do not so advertise onr fraternity. On the Fourth of Jnly, and other national occasions, it seems to me out of
character to appear otherwise than as simple citizens, As such, it is our happy privilege to appear and participate in festivities befitting the occasion. Then we are
citizens of the proudest nation of the earth, and should desire no higher rank or con·
dition. As citizens, we are all equal, and should not distinguish ourselves by any
badge or rank of fraternity. On occasions of festivity, as at Masonic balls, it seems
to me to be in exceeding bad taste for brethren to appear in Masonic clothing. The
white apron, in its place, is the appropriate and emblematic badge of a Mason;
but in a ball-room, nothing could look much more absurd and out of good taste. Let
us be quiet and unostentatious in our relations with the world, and it will respect u;;
quite n.s much as if we seek its favor by idle show.
At our last Communication, a proposition in regard to the Masonic Temple of' this
city, was referred to a special committee with instructfl'.Jns :" Ftrst, To prepare a report upon the whole subject, and furnish each Lodge under
this jurisdiction with a copy thereof, on or before the first day of July, 1865;
" Second, To receive all communications from the subordinate Lodges in relation
thereto ; and
" Third, To report the result of their labors to thiK Grand Lodge, on the second
day of it.q next Annual Communication."
The primary object of the reference was that, through the re11ort of the committee, the Lodges might be fully informed in regard to the merits of the proposition,
and each decide for itself in favor of or against it, and instruct its representatives
accordingly. I understand tliat the committee have performed their duty,and that
the representatives of the Lodges have come here with instructions to guide their
action. My own views on the subject were fully expressed in my addross last year,
and it is unnecessary to repeat them at this time. By the resolution referring tlie
subject, the committee were instructed to prepare and send out their report on or hefore the first day of July last. Sometime in Fe bmary or March, preceding, a circular
was sent out to all the Lodges of the State by Unfon Lodge, No. 58, setting forth itH
reasons against the proposition, and inviting immediate action upon it on the part of
the Lodges and a correspondence upon the subject with that Lodge. The Grand
Lodge Jiad directed how, by whom, and at what.time the subject should be bronglit
to the attention of the Lodges; and it seemed to me an act of insubordination on tJ1e
part of any Lodge to attempt to take the matter under its direction and determine the
action of the Lodges in advance of the rt' port of the committee. I directed a circular
to be sent to the Lodges, advising that they should delay taking any action upon the
proposition, until the committee should have made their report. Under almost any
other circumstances I should have arrested the charter of any Lodge that should so
far have forgotten its duty and allegiance as did Un:ion Lodge iu this case. I was
aware that considerable feeling had been exhibited in opposition to the proposition
when it was first introduced here. I had expressed my own decided approbation of'

regularity. No dissatisfaction with their then Masonic head induced this step, and

lections of their motlier of California ; and, as she will doubtless cheerfully and
warmly welcome her daughter of the Silver State as one of the Grand Lodgo sister·

11 sense. In several instances applications have hccn mat!c for pcrmi~sion to remove

literally, he has always answered that in such cases no action but th.at of the Lodge
itself was necessary. The law says that" no Lodge shall remove its place of meeting from that named in its dispensation or charter, unless," &c., &c., and as the name
of the city; town, or village is the only " place " mentioned in either of those instru·
ments, it is only a removal from, and not within, such place which can require the
proceedings prescribed in that portion of our Constitution providing for such cases.
The subject is presented here, that the Grand Lodge may correct the opinions given
by the undersigned, if they shall be deemed erroneous.

'rhe ninth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Canada was held at the
City of Hamilton, commencing on the thirteenth day of July, 1864. The M.-. lV.-.
'I'. DOUGLAS HARRINGTON was Grand Master, and the R.·.
THOMAS B. HARRIS
11 mlld Secretary. One hundred and eleven chartered Lodges, and eight under dis1w11sation, were represented.

The Address of the Grand Master is a well written paper, in which is noticed and
commended to tl1e Joyal congratulation of the Craft, the birth of a son to the Prince
of Wales; and the hope is expressed that the good Queen may be consoled in a measure for the death of her Royal Consort, by the birth of this new scion of the Royal
English tree. During the year, eight dispensations had been granted, and one re.
fused, for want of proper recommendation. Two of the Lodges-Nos. 10 and 63were consolidated by hls leave, and the Warrant of No. 63 was surrendered and canceled.
As the Grand Lodge in 1861 dispensed with the Committee and Reports on For·
eign Correspondence, a good portion of the Address is devoted to a review of the
doings of several of the Grand Lodges. He complains, and very justly, we think, of
the treatment received at the hands of the Grand Lodge of England in the matter of
a Lodge within the jurisdiction of the Grand I,odge of Canada which acknowledges
allegiance to the Mother Grand Lodge, and refuses to come under the authority of
his Grand Lodge. The Grand Lodge of Canada had declared Lodge No. 643-440 ir·
regular, and the Grand Lodge of England insists that it never ceased to be a regular
Lodge under her jurisdiction, inasmuch as the members were not unanimous in the
surrender of the Warmnt at the time of the formation of the Grand J_,ouge of Canada. The evidence of this want of unanimity was requested by Grand Muster HAR·
mNGTON, and refused by the Colonial Board, on the very ftim~y ground that, to do so,
would only open a settled question. That is about as cool as things generally get to
be, even in Canada; and the Grand Lodge takes it coolly, adopting the report of the
Committee, who say :"The Grand Lodge of England must necessar!lybe the proper jndge of its own relation towards its subordinate Lodges, and as it claims that the St. George's Lodge,
No. 64il-440, has been working regularly under it from 1856, previously to the recog·
nition of the Grand Lod~e of Canada by the Grand Lodge of England, vour Board
nre of opinion that this Grand Lodge mnst now moot cheerfully recognize ,~i. Georqe's
Lodge, notwithstanding the grounds they had previously understood to e:idst against
such recognition."
The Grand Master either felt more sensibly the difficulties and dangers arising
from a divided jnrfadiction, or was freer from the feoling of allegiance to tlie old
country, which still holds the Provinces in bondage. If tl1e Grand Lodge of England
may maintain Lodges within the jurisdiction of Canada, what hinders any other
G:rand Lodge from invading that jurisdiction? We are very much mistaken if the
Grand Lodge of Canada docs not very soon come to the eonclnsion t11at it is not safe
to tolerate within her territory any Lodges except such as l1old warrants from her·
self; and the sooner the recommendation of Grand Master HARRINGTON is adopted,
that a time be fixed when the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Canada must become absolute and exclusive within her tenitorial bounds, and notice be given of
that determination, the better it will be for her prosperity and peace.
Appropriate notice is taken of the decease of the ,V.·. W.·. Brother, the Duke of
Athol, Grand Master of Scotland, and also of the project of erecting a monument to
the late M.·. W.-. Pm1,1J' C. TucKEB, of Vermont, to aid which he ordered a contri·
bution from the funds of tlrn Grand Lodge. Other Grand J,odges are fraternally noticed, and a fow words spoken in a kindly spirit of our national disturbances. This
is not the place for ns to discuss such matters, but we may be permitted to protest
against the fearful strife of the last four years being belittled to the dimensions of a
mere "political struggle." Many matters of local interest are mentioned and commented upon. He recommends the repeal of the constitutional provision prohibiting
the election of a Master for more than two successive terms, and also the rule rc(1uiring application for the degrees to be ma(le to the J,odgc nearest the petitioner's
residence. In the revised constitution which was completed at this Communication,
no limit seems to be made as to the reelection of a Master, but the provision concerning the residence of applicants for degrees, is, we think, very wisely retained.

The committee to draft resolutions conccming the death of Grand Master l'AGI~,
reported through Past Grand Master STAN~Bl'RY. We esteem ourself happy in having
personally known Bro. PAGJ~, and we can testify that all the committee so well say of
him is but deserved praise. He was a" good man and true," in the best sense, and deservedly stood high in the esteem of the community of which he was a citizen, and of

'·None knew him but to love him,"

and our sister has lost a noble son, on whom her honors were well bestowed, and
the Fraternity at large a most dear brother, who JC warm, large heart was the abode
of that charity which is not bounded by sectarian or party lines, nor yet by the borders of Time, but wl1ich, o'crleaping all limits, embraces the whole brotherhood of
man, and reaches into the boundless realms of the eternal years.
During the session, the M.-. W.". Gl:o. C. WIIITING, presiding, decided, in answer
to a question, that it was immaterial through what channel a summons was sent, or
at what time it was received; and that, when received, if it was possible for the
brother summoned to arrive at the designated place by the time appointed, he was
bound to regard it. We do not like this indefinite style of doing things. 'rite penalty
for disobedience to a snmmons, is the highest known to Masonic law. Let us have
some fixed method of service, properly regulated by circumstances. Tf the brother
is within the jurisdiction of the Lodge from which the summons iBsues, let it be
serve<] personally by the Tyler; if he be without the jurisdiction, and his residence
be known, let summons be sent by mail,. directed to his Post Office, and sufficient
time be named in it, within which, after reception, it mu•t be obeyed. We llonot need
to take snap-judgment of our brethren. A decision was reserved to some future
time as to whether an Entered Apprentice who had lost a leg subsequent to initiation, and wore a cork substitute, could receive the degrees of Fellow Craft and Master
Mason. We shall look with interest for the decision, as we have elsewhere expressed an opinion upon a very similar case.

'l'he journal of tlte proceedings of this Grand Lodge is a record of the forty-sixth
Annual Communication. liegun and held at Indianapolis, on the twenty-fourth, twen·
ty·fifth, and twenty-sixth days of May, 1864. The M:. W.-. WrtLIA:ll HACKER was
Grand Master, and the R:. W:. FRANCI~ KING, Grand Secretary.
'fhe Address of the Grand Master is 11bly written, and occupies twenty-three
pages of the printed proceedings, its topics being arranged nuder appropriate headings. It commences with a defence of the Fraternity from the charge of being
" played out," instancing the charities of the institntion as proof " that Masonl'y
has not yet quite outlived her day; that the time to abandon her organization lms
not yet come. For while there is the widow's wail to hush, the orphan's tear to dry,
the disconsolate to comfort, the distressed of every kind to relieve, Masonry will
have enough to do to justify the continuance of her organization and demand the
exercise of all her energies."
Several halls were dedicated and corner-stones laid during the year; dispensations were issued to open thirteen new Lodges, besides five for holding military
Lodges in connection with the several Inuiana regiments in the field; Heven applica·
tions for dispensations to open new J;otlges were refused and referred to the Grand
Lodge. Several cases of discipline are reported, two of which have have geucrnl
interest for the Craft. Jn the first case, a Louge had made a Mason of 0110 who, from
physical defects, was unable to conform to the rerpiirements of the ritual. The
Grand Master promptly used
authority, bnt upon subsequent investigation dismissed tije charge against tl1e Lodge. He says, in reporting the case:It is the opinion of many among us, that Masonry, being now only speculative, it
therefore matters not what the physical defects of un applicant may be, ii' he is mentally an<l morally right, he iH a fit sulljcct to be made a Mason. Acting upon this
principle, many of the Lodges p11y but little attention to an applicant's vhysbal de·
fects. Although our laws, as they now stand, were made many ycacs since, y.:t this
matter has been winked at, and suffered to go on from year to year, without ever
being called in question. 'fhese things ought not so to be."

'V'

So thought the Grand Lodge, which adopted the report of the Committee on Jurisprudence, in which arc quoted the Old Regulation, and the decisions of several
Grand Lodges, affirming the necessity of physical perfectness on the part of the applicant for the mysteries of Masonry. 'fhat the ancient regnlation required that the
candidate for Mu.>'onry should he free from physical rlefccts, arlmits of no question.
Some Grand Lodges, owing to the speculative character of the ~'ratcrnity, have been
rlisposed to relax the rigor of the rnle in some measure, interpreting it to mean, free·
dom from such defect• as wonl<l render the candi(late unable to conform literally to
the requirements of the work and lectures of the several degrees. The;;c we be·
lieve were the views of Bro. 'fuCKEW, of Vermont. We fear any relaxation of the
rule, >wd confess to a prejudice in favor of our earlytea·ching, tlmt the candidate
wlio knocks ut the door of Masonry must be hale and sound, not dismembered at
the time of making; " a man, free born, of lau.ifu.l age, and sounrl, in body and
mind." A vast amount of trouble would be saved by adhering strictly to the letter of the law as it was received from the Fathers, anti. never questioned until the
spirit of cliange of Young America, crept into our Lodges.

"'Time, the tomb-builder,' the sexton of the ages, has .added another grave to
the myriads that fill, yet crowd not, the illimitable cemetery of the past. • * *.
* * * * \Ve meet under unusual circumstances. But three times before during
the history of our Grand Lodge, has it occurred that our Masonic head, for the time
being, was not in the Grand Orient at the opening of this Most Wor~hipful Grand
Uody. Now our beloved Grand Master is without the jurisdiction, and it is left for
me, his Deputy, to occupy his seat until you shall select and install his successor.
At the head of a noblc_regiment of fraters and profanes, he has moved calmly into
the midst of the iron waltz of battle, and has devoted himself to the service of the
Goddess of Liberty."
During the eight months of his service in room of the Grand Master, he had granted three dii!pensations to open and hold new Lodges. In this jurisdiction we notice
with regret, as we have in some farther East, that large numbers of Dispensations
ure issued to make Masons in .so-called emergent cases. 1Ve fail to see any good
reason for them, and especially do we doubt the reasonableness of the excuse,
which is stated seemingly with the utmost confidence that to all it will appear abun<lant, that the applicants were soldicrH. We yield to none in respect for the brave
men who have left the comforts and endearments of home, to meet the shock of battle in their country's cause, but we do not sec any good and sufficient reason therein,
why they should be hastily admitted to the privileges of our l<'raternity. Were they
nlways soldiers? Did they never hear of Masonry until after the w11r commenced?
llili the sound of strife in.the land open their ears 'all at once to the voice of Masonic
t.eaching? Did the flash of the bayonet and the gleam of' the swort!, dispel the
1larkness which had previously obscured j from their vision tho beauties and bene lltR of the Institution? 18 there not a palpable inconsistency, if not a direct misstatement of fact, on the very face of a petition presented under such circumHtanccs?
We cannot believe that the applicantR are uninfluenced by mercenary motives, and we
am convinced that these hasty makings of Masons, like haHty marriages, will give
nl11mdant opportunity for repenting at leisure.

where they are thus" born ont of dne time," until their Masonic beards have grown.

We have not Ro understood the duty or province of the Committee on Corres
pondence, and until very lately, it certainly has not been the practice. Several of
the committees take the same ground that tile Grand Secretary of Kentucky does,
and it m\lst be confessed that· such a courae entails much less labor upon the one

Indiana and Canada have already virtually abolished the committee, and many of
the committees seem disposed to curtail the beautiful proportions of the reports
they write. We should be sorry to see this intercourse cease, but freely own that we
had rather the labor were devolved upon some other and abler brother.

The Address of the Grand Master is brief, but replete with the true Masomc spmt,
as all.the emanations from his pen are sure to be. He had granted two dispensa· ·
tions for new Lodges, one to work in the German and the other in the l~rench language. The death of a Past Grand Officer is appropriately noticed. Ill health had
compelled Bro. FELLOWS to be absent from his jurisdiction during part .of the year.
The attention of the Craft is directed to the Ancient Charges, and especially to those
which are applicable in a peculiar manner to the situation of affairs in our country,
Bro. F.ELLOWS is still watching with solicitude to prevent his craftsmen from forget·
ting that our institution is as wide as the world-" extending from East to West be·
tween North and South "-denoting its universality and " teaching us that a Mason's
charity ~hould be equally extensive." And this charity is more. than mere ah:i:s·
giving. Love exhausts not itself thus: all kindly offlc~s !low from it a.s the '.ountam.
Sympathy is the outgrowth of Love, and Benevolence is but Sympathy m action : the
mantle of 1''raternity is thrown over every one who can prove himself a true and
genuine Brother. Within our fold may all of every name and tribe unite who bow
in humble awe and reverence before the shrine of one Great God. The sons of Ish·
maeland of Isaac, the Russ, the Gaul, the Briton, and the free American, may join about
our altar, and fear no clashing of opinion. To all these, if men and manly, we g~ve
a brother's hearty welcome : ·to all others are our doors resolutely closed. Know1~g
nor sect nor party, we are one in this, and stand upon it as on an immovabl~ and mdestructible base. Bro. FELLOWS practiced what he taught, and enforced his words
by his example. The Fraternity suftered severely from the civil strife. in the States
around them and in their own jurisdiction, but report more prosper1ty than could
have been hoped for under the circumstances.

views the proceedings of twenty-nine Grand Lodges,-sixty· four volumes in all. Our
proceedings for 18Gl-'62-'63, are briefly and fraternally noticed. The Grand Lodge

The J.t.·. W.•. Grand todge of this jurisdiction met in Annual Communication at
Portland, on the first Tuesday of May, 186i, the M..·. W.·. WILLIAM P. PREBLE, Grand
Master, presiding, and the R.-. W.•, IRA BERRY being Grand Secretary.
The Grand Master's Address occupies about seventeen pages of the printed pro·
ceedings. The following extract from the opening breathes the spirit which should
animate every Masonic heart.
"Having once again, by J?en:nlssion of the Supreme Grand Architect of the Uni·
verse, come up from onr various and distinct Masonic familr. altars, to unite as one
family under the roof-tree of our Masonic mother, how forcibly must each one of us
be impressed with the infinite mercy and kindness of that Being on whom we are de·
pendent for all the blessings and comforts we enjoy, thann his inconceivable good·
ness he has withheld the dreadful fiat by which so many of our brethren have been
11ummoned to IDs more immedi&te presence, and which must in his own good time
remove each one of us from this scene of transitory pleasure, when the places that
now know us, shall know us no more forever. May our conduct and deliberations,
both here and elsewhere, be actuated by the true spirit of Masonry, so that when
the .Grand Marshal, DEA.TR, shall conduct us into IDs Lodge abo".e, we may be re·
ceived with the welcome announcement,' Well done, good and faithful servants, en·
ter ye into the Joy of your Lord."
Three dispensations were granted to open new Lodges. Thirty-one decisions on
Masonic law were reported, and were all approved except two, and those were referred to the committee on Masonic Jurisprudence. They are mostly good and correct
l'Ulings, and where dependent upon the Constitution of that Grand Lodge, are doubt·
less the law of that jurisdiction.
Tile twelfth decision is in regard to an objection made to the advancement of an
Entered Apprentice who was not" duly anil truly prepared for his initiation," hav'
ing a ring upon his finger which could not be removed without cutting or breaking,
(whether finger or ring is not stated.) The Senior Deacon was the objecting party,
but we apprehend his objection came too late. It should have been made at the
time of initiation, and not at the time application was made foradvancement. There
is abundant opportunity given, as we all very woll know, for ·the discovery of want
of proper preparation, and at any stage of the work in the first section, if a candi·
date is found to be not" duly and truly prepared," his progress ought to be arrested
until the error is rectified. lf the Senior Deacon know the ring was on the finger of
the candidate, and failed to answer truly, informing the Master, he was remiss in his
duty; and If the Master knew the fact, he was also criminally negligent. But we
do not see that this could form any good objection to the passing of the candidate.
The error arose from no fault of Ills, unless wearing a ring at all be a fa.ult in a man,
:for he could not be supposed to know the requirements of the work; though if he
were an intelligent and observant man, he must have seen manifest inconsistency in
parts of the work and lectures. The conduct of the Sonior Deacon, to say the least,
was disingenuous; for we judge from one of the questions, that the matter of the
ring was a blind- a mere excuse to hide other objections arising out of the acts of
the candidate while a profane. Bro. PREllLE says :"Grand Master HIRAM CRASE having decided in a somewhat similar case that the
ring must be cut oft', or the candidate could not be admitted, although it ls more
11trictly following the Jetter than the spirit of Masonry, undoubtedly the objection
would have been sufficient before the candidate's Initiation. He should have made
his objection then. But having consented to his admission into the only degree in
which allusion is made in the work to metallic substances, such an objection b~comes
puerile in the ·other degrees."
Especially, the Grand Master might have added, when it was known that in the
mean time the ring had been removed. " The letter and spirit of Masonry" we may
be allowed to say, are so closely and intimately connected as to admit of no separa·
tion. The regulation, of which the brother speaks, bas solemn and impressive meaning- conveys a lesson of the gravest moment, in which the peace and harmony, and
hence the very strength of the institution rests. Masonry teaches by symbols, and

1865.]

the symbolic language must be preserved in its purity, that it may have ita full force
and effect in and upon the mind of the neophyte.
The twenty-first decision is :" A Mason can properly avouch for another only after having eat in a Lodise of
Master Masons with him, or as one of the committee appointed by the Worshipful
Ma•ter to examine him. The practice of undertaking to examine a person (claiming
to lie a Mason,) except when sl/ecially appointed for that purpose by the Master, is a
vury dani;erous and reprehensible one. The danger arises from the fact that the
Worshipful Master cannot draw a distinction between the members of his Lodge·
1111<1 if he allows one to do it, he can scarcely deny the same privilege to another'
who, although entirely incompetent, believes himself to be best qualified."
'
This strikes us as entirely too strict a construction. There may be proof as irre·
fragable as that of having sat In a Master Mason's Lodge with a man. Confining the
phrase " legal information" within such narrow limits may be very well, but we do
not so understand it.

Proceedings of the

State is not even prima facie evidence that either ls extinct. The brother had better
wait until by the opening of communication he can obtain the proper evidence of
good standing and withdrawal. Nor do we see that a man's being a soldier, gives
him any peculiar claim upon the Fraternity, or that our laws should be suspended for
his benefit and convenience, any more than for that of another man, who may be every
way more worthy. In the other matter however, we cannot say we quite agree with
him. Our Grand Lodge, like that of Maine, does not require that a brother must
have served as a Warden before he can be elected Master. There was a time in the his·
tory of Freemasonry, when the Grand Master needed only to have been a Fellow Craft
before his election; and so far as our Constitution is concerned, we conceive that
any Master Mason, being a member in good standing of some Lodge in this jurisdic·
diction, might be elected Grand Master. Many times, if the rule of Maryland obtain,
ed, a Lodge would be compelled to pass over a very competent brother on the tloor,
and take 11. very incompetent Warden from the West or South. We see no common
sense in such a course, and know of no good reason why a Grand Lodge may not
make a new regulation in regard to this matter, as well as in reference to the trial.of
a Grand Master. Let merit and competency be the rule of preferment among us as
Masons.
In his review of Oregon, Bro. WROTH mentions the jurisdictional difference which
had arisen with the Grand Lodge of Washington Territory, and agrees with the Grand
Master of Oregon in his view of the matter.

MASSACHUSETTS.
Two pamphlets containing the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts
for the years 1863-1864, have been received.
We discover in the proceedings for 1863 nothing of general interest or importance.
The following statistics are takeh from the Report of the M:. W:. Grand Master, at
the Anniversary Communication in December.
Whole number of Lodges, 124; Army Lodges, 11; whole number initiated, 1700;
dispensations granted, 125; whole number of affiliated Masons, 10,000. Three new
Halls were dedicated by the Grand Master.
The journal for 1864, contains the proceedings from March 9, to December 27,
1864, being the one hundred and thirty-first Anniversary.
The Quarterly Communication was held in September. A committee made a full
and learned report upon a proposed change in the Constitution, prohibiting the
'making of more than five candidates at one session. The law and usage is fully examined, and the committee say:"Your committee therefore believe that the proposed amendment is not a change
in the Masonic usage, but is simply restoring the c.onstitutions, rul~s, and regu!ations,
which have been recognized as such from the earliest days of written Masomc Con·./
iltitutions."
The following amendment was passed:"No Lodge shall hold more than one communication on the same day, nor confer
either of the three degrees upon more tha1,1 five candidates at one communi~atio!l·
No Lod"e shall permit more than one candidate to be present at the same time, m
the first"section of the first degree, nor in the second section of the third degree."
A Special Communication was held in October, for the purpose of laying the co1"
ner·stone of the new Masonic Temple, intended to take the place of the one destroyed
by fire in the preceding spring. The array of Lodges and other Masonic bodies was
imposing, and the gathering of distinguished Masons was never equalled perhaps in
this country. There were eighteen bands of music in the procession.
"The march began at about twelve o'clock, and the processi?n moved at quick
step • passed over the route in a little less than two hours - startmg from the Com·
man; as above, and passing through Winter, Summer, Otis, Devonshire, Milk, Broad,

Grand Lodge ef OaUfornla,

1865.J

f!tate, Court, Tremont, and Beacon Streets, and entering the ComnUln at Charles
Street Mall, thence passing through Beacon Park and Tremont Street Malls to the
Mite of the new Temple. The whole distance was perhaps three miles • and it was
observe~ that when the rear portion of the process10n was leaving the dommon the

In regard to granting dispensations to confer degrees, our Michigan brother adopted
the~e four rules : " To deny all applications-First: Where the candidate was.under twenty-one
years of age, (under any circumstances.") [The Grand Master, his predecessor, had
granted such a dispensation to a soldier-boy, alleging that there was no regulation
forbidding it.] " Second : Wl1ere the candidate had resided many years in the
vicinity of a Lodge, and had made no application for admission, until he was about
to leave home, showing clearly that he. was influenced by selfish, mercenary motives,
(without good reason being given to the contrary.) Thir'd: Where the candidate
does not reside (legally) within the jurisdiction of the Lodge applying. Fonrlh:
Showing some strong reason why the time prescribed by the Constitution and edicts
should be dispensed with."
Bro. MOORE differs with Bro. MACKEY in regard to the powers and privileges of
Lodges under dispensation, and presents some very cogent reasons for his views. He
does not believe that Masons made in military Lodges are" made in a regularly consti·
toted Lodge," and does not recognise them as :1.iasons entitled to visit. He regards
Army LGdges as trespassers upon the jurisdiction of sister Lodges. In both tl1eRe
last positions, we are very much inclined to side with him. Some nice qµestions will
arise oot of these things In the time to come, and it is well for os to be thinking
about them. The Grand Master has been in search of the true work, and has consulted a number of the Great Lights, and, from what he sa.ys, we suppose he thinks he
has found it. He decides more thun once, that spreading the ballot a second time
is a prerogative of the Master, needing no rule of the Constitution of the Grand
Lodge or by-laws of a Lodge to authorize it. We are sticklers for all the rights of
the Masters of Lodges, but see no harm from the regulation of this matter by a
Grand Lodge. There is quite a list of decisions on Masonic law, and, after carefully
coilllidering them, we think Bro. lfooRE is right. We have conceived a very strong
liking to this M.-. W.·. Brother. We should like to extend our arm over the moun·
tains, and give him a good, hearty, brotherly grip. He writes with the prQmpt,
earnest tone of a man who had 11 soul, and threw it into his work.

The Grand Lodge assembled in Annual Communication, June 8, 1864, at the city
of Concord. The 1lf.'. W.-. CnARLES H. BELL presided, and delivered 11 short address,
in which he assures the Grand Lodge that the prosperity had not been diminished ;
he sees danger in the rapid growth of the institution, from the application and admission of improper persons; had granted a few, and refused a number of di;;pcnsations in emergent cases; does not think the last Semi-Annual Session as profitable as
usual ; warns again!lt the introduction of topics calculated to stir up strife by induc-~
ing discussion; mentions appropriately the death of Past Grand l\faster HuGHEB, and
two other brethren; reports one dispensation granted to open a new Lodge, and
peremptorily declines a reClection.
The committee appointed to examine and report upon the matter of work, attended to their duty thoroughly, and present an able and interesting report. The
conclusion to which they come is, th11t the work already established and sanctioned
by the Grand Lodge, is good enuugh, and th11t Ron. MORRIS and his "Mnemonics "
are not to be trusted.
We were surprised in ·reading the report of the Committee on Grievances in one
case, at the result to which they came. It is not our province, of course, to interfere
with discipline, but onr brethren will permit us to express an opinion in a kindly
aud friendly way, tbat the Lodge at Wilton deserved to have its charter arrested,
quite as much as the member who was expelled deserved that sentence. If he was

We learn, with pleasure, that our good brother of Maryland was made glad at
heart and in pocket by means of the contribution from this Grand Lodge ; and we
trust that his·labor.s among those to whom he was sent were crowned with abund·
ant success.
We cannot too hlghly commend the care and zeal displayed by the Grand Secretary in his attention to the increase of our library, both in the number of its volumes
and in the value and character of the works obtained; and the hearty tha~ks of this
Grand Lodge are due to Bro. S. C. PERKINS, of Pennsylvania, and Bro. WILLIAM L.
MAITLE, of Virginia, for their kindness in co-operating with and aiding that officer in
his efforts to make ours the best and most complete Masonic library on the continent.
We most sincerely trust that the hope expressed by the Grand Secretary in this
connection, may indeed be realized, and that the kindly intercourse, once existing

To the M.-. W. ·. Grand Lodge of <Jolifornia :~
Your committee, to whom was referred the resolution relative to the amount due
Hiram Loftge, No. 43, from the Representative Fund for the year 1862, respectfully
report: That the proceedings at the Annual Communication of that year show that
the Junior Warden of the aforesaid J,odge was then its delegate to the Grand Lodge,
but that the Lodge paid no dues for that year. Under the General Regulation, No.
14, relative to the payment of representatives, it is stated that " no delegate shall
receive such payment whose Lodge shall not have paid its dues for the current
year." Consequently, none was called for by the delegate. Since that period, however, owing to a resolution from the Committee on Jurisprudence, found on page 337
of the proceedings of 1864, the Lodge has paid to this Grand body its entire indebtedness. Believing, therefore, that the Lodge should be reimbursed, from the
Representative Fund, for the traveling expenses of its representative in the year
1862, and that such action will not conflict with our former financial precedents, your
committtee recommend tlie adoption of the resolution, as follows :~
Resolved, That the Grand Secretary is hereby instructed to draw an order ou the
Grand Treasurer for thirty dollars in behalf of Ifiram Lodge, No. 43, being the
amount due its delegate to the Grand Lodge in 1862.
All wl1ich is respectfully submitted.
ISAAC S. TI'l'cS,

Bro. HENRY H. RHEES, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, pre.
sented the following reports:To the M. •• W. ·• Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, having considered the matters contained in the report of the
Grand Secretary which were referred to them, report as follows:
Jn the matter of special dispensations to re ballot and to elect officers, they find
the petitions for such dispensations to be in due form and to comply in every respect
with the requirements of the Constitution, and therefore recommend the approval by
this Grand Lodge of the issue of said dispensations.
In the matter of the removal of a Lodge from the place of meeting named in its
dispensation or charter, they are of the opinion that the language of Sec. 1, Art. Ill,
Part III, of the Constitution, will bear no other construction than that which is given
to it by the Grand 'secretary. They therefore recommend the adoption by the Grand
Lodge of the view so expressed, that the Constitution prohibits removal from the
town or city in which a Lodge is located, and not removal from one hall to another
within such town or city.
All which is respectfully submitted.

To the M. ·. W. •. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee have considered the decisions of the Grand Master, on points of
Masonic 1!1w, and report as follows:In the matter of a candidate whose initiation is prevented by objection after his
"election but before receiving the first degree, under the provisions of Sec. 5, Art. III,
Pa.rt III: of the Constitution, they agree with the Grand Master, that such objection 1

1865.)

Grand Lodge of Ocdifornia.

o"rmot be designed to place the candidate in a worse condition, as regards Ma·
•nnry, than a rejection by ballot. If the objection stays his initiation forever, unless
wlthclrawn, one who has objections to him may simply stay away from the Lodge
mnutlng, allow him to be elected, and then interpose an objection to his initiation ;
•rul not only the door of that Lodge, but the door of every other is closed against
him to the end of time. Your committee cannot think this was ever intended
~'ho the operation of the law, and they recommend the approval of the 'decision,
Ll111t the candidate may apply to that Lodge, or any other within whose jurisdiction
hn may be, at the expiration of twelve months, as though he had been rejected by
l1111lot.
In the matter of the effect of a reversal by the Grand Lodge of a judgment ·Of
•n•peusion or expulsion, your committee agree with the Grand Master, that the ac·
nnMcHI is at once restored to the standing he had before charges were preferred. If
lhlM ho not so, t)ie appeal and the judgment of reversal are simply solemn farces.
'l'hu reversal, in terms, declares that the charges were untrue or unsupported by evi11.rwo, and the judgment founded thereon unwarranted, and of course, unjust. Its
•11\Jut is to put the brother appealing in precisely the position he occupied before the
11lmrges were preferred. Bro. MACKEY, on this point, well says: "When a Lodge has
wrongfully deprived a Mason of his membership by expulsion from the Order, the
llrnncl Lodge, on his appeal, if it shall find the party is innocent,. that wrong has been
Inflicted, that, by the sentence, the laws of the institution as well as the rights of the
lt11llviclual, have been violated, may, on his appeal, interpose and redress the wrong,
11ot only by restoring him to his rights and privileges as a Mason, but also to mem·
h111·"Jlip in the Lodge. This, it seems to me, is the true principle, not only of Masonic
law, but also of equity. If a brother be innocent, he must be restored to everything
or which an unjust sentence had deprived him-to membership in his Lodge, as well
•• to the general rights of Masonry."
Bro. ALBERT PIKE, on the same point, uses this language :" lf on appeal, the Grand Lodge reverses the decision of the subordinate, on the
11ruuncl of error in the proceedings, or innocence, that reversal annuls the judgment,
111111 it is as if never pronounced-non avenu; consequently, it has no effect what1•v11r, and in Masonic law, the matter stands as if no such judgment had ever been
1·1•111iured. The accused is not restored to the Order or to membership. The effect
or rnversal is that he never was suspended or expelled at all, in law ; and there is no
1111wcr in the Grand Lodge, either by the judgment or previous legislation, to give
•ul'l1 ,indgment any other or less effect. If the Grand Lodge tries the case demovo
11111l 11cljudges the party innocent, of course, it must annul the judgment of the sub·
nrollnate Lodge in toto : and if the suspension from membership resulted solely from
I/wt judgment, there never was, in law, any suspension."
According fully in opinion with these views, your committee recommend the ap11roval of the decision of the Grand Master.
Ju the matter as to who may take an appeal from the judgment of a commission
rur trial, they are of opinion that the language of the law excludes every one save
llw accuser and the accused. By operation of law the judgment of a majority of
lhn commissioners becomes the judgment of the Lodge; and it was never yet heard
llrnt a court rendering judgment in a case might turn about and appeal to a higher
t•onrt, from its own judgment. They recommend the approval of the action of the
llmucl Master in ordering the judgment in the case to which he refers to be carried
l11to effect.
In the matter of qualification of candidates, the committee agree in the propriety
ur r11publishing the rule reported last year upon this subject, and recommend that it
ho published as a Regulation. By reference to it, it will be seen that lt makes capahlllty to read and write one of the qualifications necessary in a candidate, and, in
11111 view of the committee, very properly so. It has been well said, that "a slug11l•h ncquiescence in a condition of ignorance is incompatible with the scientific aims
uf M11~onry" ; and if a man has lived to maturity, or beyond that period, in contented

be admitted to the brighter light of Masonry. It may \vell be doubted whether such

In the matter of the question of Bro. McKuNE, but one answer can be given.
There is no appeal from the ruling of a Grand Master. The authorities and the reasoning may be found fully set forth by MACKEY, in his Masonic Jurisprudence, where
he gives not only his own -.;iews, but those of some of the ablest Masonic jurists in the
country; and the question has already been decided by this Grand J,odge, vide pages
108 and 109, Vol. I, of our Proceedings.

In the matter of the inquiry of Bro. FUQUA, your committee are of opimon that during the period of suspension for unmasonic conduct, the dues of a brother should
cease. He is under a disability from which he cannot, of his own will, free himself.
When suspended simply for non-payment of dues, he is in a position from which he
may, by his own act, at any time relieve himself, and he should pay his dues accordingly. But ~bile he is under suspension for unmasonic conduct, he is cut off entirely
from all privileges, and can only be restored by an act of his Lodge, or of the Grand
Lodge. They answer, then, that a Mason suspended for non-payment of dues, and
subsequently suspended for unmll!lonic conduct, should be charged dues only during
the period 'when he was under suspension for non·payment thereof.

Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. E. A. McCULLOUGH
from the action of St. John's Lodge, No. 37, in suspending him from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry, have had the same under consideration, and report that
the evidence docs not sustain the specification on which the accused was found
guilty and suspended. Though it does not show that the accused advised the candi.
date to withdraw his petition, as he was sure to be blackballed, it does show th~t
he conversed with the candidate as to the likelihood of his being blackballed. This
certainly was very reprehensible, and had the specification been in accordance with
the facts, a little wholesome punishment in the case might have proved advantageous
to the Craft generally, by the lesson it would teach of the necessity of abstaining ,
from all conversation with a candidate as to the action upon his petition. Your
committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution :Resol·ved, That the judgment of St. John's Lodge, No. 37, suspending Bro. E. A.

Hy the course pursued in this case, a precedent has been established that must

[Oct. 13,

judgment without appealing; or, having appealed, where the sentence h~s been
confirmed, and they are cut off from all Masonic favor unless their Lodge: or the
Grand Lodge extends forgiveness and restores them. Su9h cases are not very
rare. A good man may yield to temptation in an unguarded moment, and .sacri· ,
flee the fair name of years. His offence may be such that Mn.sonic cognizance must
be taken of it, and Masonic punishment visited. But if that punishment [takes the
form of suspension, and afterwards the erring brother evinces, by all good works
meet for repentance, that he hns recovered his moral stnnding, and perhaps by
years of such good deeds amply atones for his fault, shall not he have mercy if he
asks it of those whose creed is brotherly love? To whom shall he apply except to
the Lodge which judicially ascertained his fault, whose records contain the best evi· '
deuce of his Masonic history, and whose members have the best means of knowing
tlie sincerity of his repentance? If that Lodge rejects his application he l!lay still
be heard here ; and the resolution provides that he shali give notice of his intended
application here to the subordinate J,odge, that that Lodge may present its reasons
for refusing mercy, to be weighed by the Grand Lodge. If the subordinate Lodge
grants the petition, the necessity of a hearing in the Grand Lodge ceases. We can
not conceive of a better system to reach such cases, and grant clemency whenever
it becomes a Masonic duty, and yet guard against e:i; parte representations and nn·
founded sympathetic appeals in the Grand Lodge.
Your committee see no force in the objection that it is humiliating to a brother, SUS·
pended by a Lodgjl, to compel him to ask that J,odge for restoration befora.applying
here. Every presumption is in favor of the regularity of the action of the subordi·
nate Lodge in conducting trials. Certainly it is not to be p1·esumed that the Lodge,
iu trying and suspending a brother, is governed by prej(\!iice, or anything except
justice and Masonic law. If injustice is done to the accused he can appeal to the
Grand Lodge under another branch of our jurisprudence, and regain his rights. Such
being the presumption, aud such his safeguard ,against in,fustice, there .can be no·
thing humiliating to a brother who desires to be restored to the bosom of a Lodge, to
request the favor of that Lodge. But, by such application being enforced, we gain
the advantage that there is Jess liability of an improvident exercise of the power of
restoration than by any other system. For these reasons the committee recommend·
the adoption of the general regulation as presented.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Your committee have had before them the following question propounded by
Bro. FI."QUA :~
"Jn cases of trial, when one or more of the commissioners is absent, can a quo·
rum proceed to the trial of the case and render judgment, or must the Master
appoint to fill vacancies?"
It has been more than once decided already, that a quorum of the commissioners
may proceed to trial and judgment, but that, in such case, the judgment must be tliat
of a majority of all the commissioners elected, to wit: if the number of the com·
missioners be seven, four may try the case-but all four must concur in the judg·
ment. N 0 power is anywhere conferred upon the Master to appoint members to fill
vacancies.

Bro. JAMES L. ENGLISll, from a minority of the same committee, preeented the following report::lb the M.•. W.·. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. Jo:e:N RoBINllTT, from
the action of Oorrlaental Lodge, No. 22, in suspending him from all the rights and

[Oct. 14,

privileges of Masonry, have had the same under consideration, and the undersigned
respectfnlly report as follows :The charge is that the accused black-balled candidates from improper motives.
"A Mason is responsible to no human powtir for the vote that he casts on.the
f!etition of a candidate. 'To his own eonscience alone is he to answer for the motives
that have led to the act, and for the act itself. It is of course wrong, in the exer·
else of this invaluable right, to be ~uenced by pique or prejud!ce,
by ll;n adverse
vote, to indulge an ungenerous feeling. But, whether a member is or is not m~uenced
by such motives, or is indulging such feelings, no one bas a right to inqmre. No
Mason can be ·called to an account for the vote that he has deposited. A Lodge is
not entitled, indeed, to know how any one of its members has voted. No inquiry on
this subject can be entertained-no information can be received."
This is the law upon the subject as laid down by that able llfasonic jurist, Bro.
ALBERTG.MACKEY. But, though "no inquiry on the subject can be entertained," yet
as it is " wrong, in the exercise of this invaluable right, to be influenced by improper
motives," if a case should ever occur in which a brother avowed that be had black·
balled a candidate from motives which were clearly improper, your committee are
of the opinion that it would be an offence punishable by the proper Masonic authority. It must, however, be a case in which the motives are distinctly avowed, and
nothing must be left to inquiry or inference.
Judging the case now under consideration by these mies, we cannot see how the
judgment can be sustained. We have' searched the record diligently, and find no
distinct avowal by the accused of any improper motive. The sentence should there·
fore be reversed. We cannot dismiss this ease, however, without calling the attention of the Grand Lodge to the following violations of the law of the ballot which are
disclosed' in its record:1st. A brother deposits his ballot in such a manner that it can be seen how he
votes: 2d. One brother looks to see how another brother votes : 3d. One brother
tells how another brother votes: 4th. One brother accuses another of casting a b~ack
ball: 5th. One brother asks another why he blackballed the candidate : 6th.· The
Master calls a brother to the east and inquires· of him if he cast a black ball, and
why he did it.
These are all offences against the law of the ballot, and punishable, for " nothing
must be done to impair the inviolable secrecy of the ballot."
Your committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, That the action of Oc<iidenlal, Lodge, No. 22, in suspending Bro. JonN
RollINETT from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby
reversed and set aside.
All which is respectfully submitted.
HENRY HARE HARTLEY,

The W.·. ADDISON C. NILES, Grand Orator, then delivered the Annual
Oration, as follows:MosT W OBSlIIPFUL GRAND MASTER
AND BRETHREN OF TRE GRAND LODGE:At our last annual meeting, the office I have the honor to hold was vacant. The
appointment of our Most Worshipful Grand Master had been annulled by the fiat of
the Highest. The silver voice that had once spoken to us within these walls-how

1805.]

Grand Lodge ef California.

125

doquently, you remember-of Masonic charity and order, was hushed and still.
Your Orator had been called to a higher place in the Lodge beyond the stars. He
tlied, as a servant of his master should, in the midst of earnest work for Him.
"The great work laid upon his two score years
Is done, and well done. If we drop our tears,
Who loved bim as few men were ever loved,
We mourn no blighted hope nor broken plan
With him whose life sta.nds rounded and approved
In the full growth and stature of a man."
I could have wished that the choice of our Grand Master had fallen upon some
one worthier to b1·eak the spoil that lingers here. But I even cannot stand whcro
he stood, and not feel something of the leading principle of his noble life-that always the worthiest thing to do is duty, and that one should bring to the performance
of every appointed task the best ability he may.
We are not, brethren, the representatives of Masonry. r'\. representative has
power to change, to modify, to reform. In this sense, Masonry has no representa·
tives. It has exponents of its principles and plans. All over the world-on battle·
liclds, by the side of the sick and dying, by the burial-place of the dead, beneath the
roof of the widow and the orphan, close at the ear of the erring, wherever is sin or
sorrow-the principles of Masonry find expression in relief or warning. Beyond
this, it delegates no powers. We are but watchmen in the outer courts of the temple, placed tliere to guard its approaches with jealous eye, to keep far away from its
portals all save good men and true, to see that none enter its sacred 1irecincts save
in the appointed way. Our authority ceases at the threshho!U. We are instructed,
first of all, that" it is not in the power of any man or body of men, to make innova·
tions on the ground-work of Masonry." Within the temple arc the jewels and orna·
monts, the altar and the lights, each in the place where it bas been since the pile
was rcarecl, as sacred from touch or change by us as by the humblest artisan. We
have not power to alter the holy teaching.i of one lesson, the solemn meaning of one
~oken or symbol. In all things belonging to the ground-work of the order, we aro
powerless to reform. In Masonry, reform is treason.
lt must be a peculiar institution, and should be a worthy one, that could make it
a prime article of its creed that through all time no change should be made in its
organic law; that can say that duriilg its long past, through all the world's marvel·
ous progress, no change has occurred in its principles or plans; that dares to say,
in the face of all the glorious probabilities of the future-it shall be as it lias been,
unchanged and unchangeable.
There are inevitable conditions to the possibility of such a permanency. The in·
Btitution that would claim it, must be from the commencement perfect and complete.
There must be in its principles no cloubtful balance of rights and wrongs, no mooted
point for the keen questioning of advancing intellect. Masonry has this qualification. From the beginning it has been but a group of the simplest virtues linked
together by the simplest symbols.
It teaches Faith, not in creeds, not in forms, but in God; the common faith of
manhood, that cannot fail to see in this broad green earth, this brave o'erhanging
firmament, in all the grand glories of the unlverse about uR, and the still small voice
within, evidence of a large intellect and larger Jove than we can know-guarding
and supporting our weak humanlty.
It teaches Truth. Not only to speak true words, but to be true men-to live lives
true in act and thought-to be true in our dealings with the. world, in our relations
with those near to us.
It teaches Brotherly Love ; that man was not meant to walk through this world
11lone. Too many devious ways, bordered by flowers and watered by pleasant
Htreams, but leading imperceptibly from the right ; too many hidden pitfalls where

•
126

Proceedings if the

[Oct. 14,

the solitary traveler might fall, and come forth sorely bruised and stained; too many
wandering soldiers of the Prince of Darkness against whose fierce assaults the
prowess of a single arm would be but weakness; too many sorrows falling, how
sadly, upon the solitary heart, needing only sympathy to change to consolation.
It teaches Charity-not merely that generous impulse that leads kind hearts
always to relieve with material aid the wants of the needy and suffering - but a
broader charity-that suifereth long and is kind-that, ever strhing earnestly, patiently, to reform, still casts its broad mantle over the faults of an erring brotherthat impels us, while as true men we are to stand unflinchingly aud to the death by
the religion we believe in, and the truth as we have received it -to leave to each
one else the determination of his duty and his faith-a question only between his
conscience and his God.
These simple vfrtnes: Faith, Truth, Love, Charity, ask no sanction from the ad·
vancing age. ·They are not light-house lamps to be overthrown and quenched by the
shifting currents of opinion, but a cluster of stars shining serenely always, because
lit and held forth by God's own hand. These lessons could be read as well in the
groves of the academy as at the feet of Jesus, or by the broad light of this high
noon of the centuries.
'l'here is an evident policy in the prohibition of any change, when we once admit
that the peculiar constitution ofl\Iasonry has rendered it possible. There is a special
charm in this immutability. It is the same charm that invests all things cl!angeless in
the midst of change. But it not only lends a eharm to Masonry. It is necessary that
an institution, aiming to be both universal and permanent, should be at all times and
everywhere identical, not only in its precepts and the form and manner of its teachings, but in the practical exemplification of its principles. It must be able to stand
by quietly and calmly, fulfilling its humane and gentle mission, not more in times
of peace and pleasantness, than when the fierce passions that attend the birth of
new ideas are swaying and controlling men. We have no need to search through
history for an example of this power. Standing in the sunlight of the great peace
that through the blessing of God has come to us, we can look calmly now upon the
terrible past, and be proud, as Masons, that the great clamor of war has never
drowned the still, small voice of Masonic charity. We all remember how; when the
conflict was fiercest, and the tide of victory swayed this way and that, every true
heart in the land, wherever its sympathies might be, was wrought to the utterest
intensity of hope or fear; so that all there was in life seemed to be involved in the
pending issue. And yet, can I not say that, iu not a single J,odge throughout our
State, has this all-absorbing passion found an utterance? Not a change proposed
that would bar one Mason anywhere from the rights of our broad brotherhood? And
even in the arena where the terrible drama was enacted, where the Titans strove in
wonderfnl conflict beneath the eyes of the world for the mastery of principles,
Masons did not forget that" they had registered words not to be unspoken or recalled,
antedating, as they will survive, all disturbances among men, and turmoils in State."
We have heard how, when a gallant sailor, a Mason, was stricken down at the post
of duty upon the deck of the Harriet Lane, his body was borne to burial at Galveston, followed by a sad procession of mourners, victors and prisoners commingledencmies before, but brethren then. Who knows how many a living soldier retains
fondly the memory of some simple Masonic charity; how many a dying soldier has found
his sacrifice of life made lighter by some unrecorded kindness at a brother's hand?
BL1t while Masonry demands of its votaries an absolute adherence to the rule that
it shall not change with any change of creed, or with the varying knowledge or belief of men, it is not conservative in the sense of interposing any obstacle to the advancement of humanity in whatever way. It is no clog upon the wheel of progress.
Because we believe in the exercise of faith, truth, brotherly love, and charity, we do
not believe that
"Earth should stand and gaze like Joshua's moon on Ajalon.''

1865.]

Grand Lodge if Ooldfornia.

127

Whenever science needs to be advanced or knowledge extended-whenever a
larger life requires a newer faith, whenever right is to be defended and wrong reclressed, wherever in the world's broad field we are called to do God's work for man,
whether it be to labor or tb fight-we can surely fulfil our calling as well,, and with a
1mrer and truer zeal, while we cherish in our heart of hearts the simple, earnest
teachings of the Lodge.
Masonry remains unchanged because it is perfect in its simplicity. And so it has
Mtood by-not aiding much, never delaying-while the imperfect world moved on
from point to point towards the happy circle of the golden year. It has watched the
11rogress of the nations, the ebb and flow of opinion through the centuries, as calmly
1md serenely as the Sphynx has sitt by Egypt, " watching like a Providence with the
H11mc earnest eyes, and the same sad, tranquil mien," the builders of the Pyramids
11.11d the wondering travellers of to-day. And yet, not like the Sphynx--stony-heart<>d, doing no good thing for man-for Masonry is beneficent always. Rather like those
mighty currents that flow beneat11 the surface of the ocean, mingling the waters of
1111 climates, regardless how the sea above may throb and beat, still keeping their
1111pointed course as on the morning of creation-unseen, resistless, but bearing to
the frozen poles the breath of summer airs, and planting upon naked coral·reefs the
Heeds of mighty palms and tropic verdure.
We who have stood within the secret place of Masonry, and received its perfect
light, know well the excellence and beauty of its lessons. We can look back proudly upon its course through time, marked with clustered and scattered blessings as
the river-banks with verdure. And for its future, if wc fulfill our sacred trust, and
pass it unchanged to those who shall succeed us, who can say how many sorrows
.wi.ll be alleviated through its kindly aid; how many snll'erings relieved, how many

PART I I I .
Of Subordinate Lodges.
ARTICLE I.
OF THE ORGANIZATION OF A LODGE.

SECTION 1. A Lodge can only be formed by authority of a dispensation from
the Grand Master, or of a charter from the Grand Lodge; and no charter shall be
granted to any Lodge, nntil it shall have worked a time uuder dispensation, and
shall have exhibited to the Grand Lodge satisfactory evidence of its Masonic capability.
Sile. 2. Upon the petition of seven or more Master Masons being presented to
the Grand Master, in the form prescribed in Art. III, Part VII, he may grant them
a dispensation to open and hold a Lodge at the place therein to be named, with.
power to make Masons and, receive members by affiliation; and he shall therein
appoint the Master and Wardens of the new Lodge. But in no case shall such dispensation be issued, unless the petition be accompanied by a recommendation from
the nearest or most convenient chartered Lodge, (if from a town or city wliere more
than one Lodge exists, then from a majority of such J,odges,) setting fol'th, iu the
form prescri~ed in Art. III, Part VII, that the petitioners are all 3'Iaster Masons in
good standing, that the establishment of the new Lodge is of manifest propriety and
will conduce to the good of the Order, and that a safe and snitable Lodge-room has
been provided therefor; nor nnless the petition sha11 also be accompanied by a cer·
tificate of withdrawal of each petitioner from the Lodge of which he was last a mem·
ber, and by a certificate from a Master, whom the Grand Master is satisfied is well
skilled ,in the craft, declaring that the ]\faster proposed in such petition is fully competent properly to confer the three degrees of Masonry, and to deliver entire the
lectures thereunto appertaining. Such dispensation shall terminate npon the first
day of the month in which the next succeeding Annual Communication shall be
holden ; and shall then be returned to the Grand Secretary, together with the by·
laws, book of records, and returns of the new Lodge to that date.
SEC. 3. Upon the return of the dispensation of a new Louge, as above, with a
petition for a charter, in the form prescribed in Art. Ill, Part VII, if an examination
of its work and proceedings shall prove satisfactory, the Grand Lodge may order the
issue of a charter to such Lodge, and assign it such name and number on the registry
as shall be deemed proper; and such Lodge shall be duly constituted within sixty
days thereafter, or its charter shall be forfeited. If the examination be not satisfactory, the petition may be totally refused, or a continuance of the dispensation, until
the next Annual Communication, may be ordered; but no such continuance shall be
granted a second time.
SEc. 4. A Lodge shall consist of a Master, a Senior Warden, a J nnior Warden, a
Treasurer, a Secretary, a Senior Deacon, a Junior Deacon, a Tyler, and snch other
officers as its by·laws may provide ; together with as many members as it may find
convenient.

will be taken, that he may, if he choose, be present thereat.
SEC. 6. The Commissioners may adjourn from time to time, at their own cdnve·
nience, or for sufficient cause shown by either party; provideJl that the period within
which their duties shall be concluded shall not exceed ten days, unleos, for good reasons shown, the Master shall grant them further time.
SEC. 7, After all the testimony shall liave been received, the Commisioners shall
proceed to deliberate upon their verdict and sentence, with none present save themselves and the Secretary, which last shall have no voice in the proceedings. The
Judgment of the majority of the Commissioners shall be taken as the d.ecision of the
whole; and when the trial is concluded, the Secretary shall make a fair copy of the
record and finding, under their supervision, which shall be signed by the chairman of
such Commission, and attested by the Secretary, and shall be presented to the Master who at the next meeting of his Lodge, shall, in the presenco of its members
only, announce the result, and direct the Secret11ry to record the same as tho judgment of the Lodge, and file the record for safe keeping among its archives.
SEC. 8. The penalties which may be inflicted are reprimand in open Lodge, suspension, or expulsion. If the sentence be reprimand, the ~foster shall summon the
adjudged to appear at the next stated meeting, when it shall be carried into effect, in
the presence only of members of the Lodge. If it be suspension or expulsion, it
shall at once go into effect, and the Secretary shall immedi11tcly notify the Grand
Secretary tJ1ereof; antlit shn.J.I be final and conclusive, unless an appeal be taken to
the Grand J,odge.
SEc. 9. An appeal may be taken to the Grand Lodge by either party, at its next
succeeding Annual Commnnication, but not unless a notice of such intended 11ppeal
shall be given to the Master within thirty diiys after his announcement of the result
of the trial ; and in all cases of expnlsiQn or suspension, the Master shall causo the
Secretary to prepare a transcript of the record of trial, and immediately transmit
it to the Grand Secretary, together with information of the appeal intended, if any
there be.
ARTICLE V.
OP REVISIONS AND ltESTORAT!ONS.
SECTION I. All judgments from which an appeal shall be taken as hereinbefore
In this Part provided, shall be reviewed in the Grand Lodge, or before a committee
thereof, during its sessions, upon the record sent up, and upon such other proper
documents as may be submitted; and it• decisions shall be final and conclusive.
SEO. 2. All sentences of suspension shall be for an indeliuite period; and a Lodge
may, at any stated meeting, by the votes of two-thirds of the members present,
annul any such sentence of suspension pronounced by itseif, and l'estore the .Mason
thus suspended to all his Masonic rights; provided that notice of a re~olution f~r
such restoration shall have been given at the stated meeting next precedmg : and m
case of such restoration, the Secretary shall at once notify the Grand Secretary
thereof.

ARTICLE I.
AMENDMENTS.
HECTION 1. Any proposed amendment to this Constitution shall be presented at
1m Annual Communication, and shall in all cases be referred to the committee on
.I uriKprudence, who shall report before a vote thereon be taken.
H1w. 2. After ,the report of said committee, if the vote in favor of such pro·
l"'"ed amendment be unanimous, it shall be declared adopted ; and from and after
l.h11 close of that Communication, shall become a part of the Constitution.
H~:o. 3. If the vote in fovor of such proposeu amendment be not unanimous, but
1.lrnre be a majority therefor, it shall lie over for one year, and shall be published with
ihu proceedings, under the caption of" Proposed Amendments to the Constitution;"
1111!1 if, at the next succeeding Annual Communication, it "hall receive two-tllirds of
I.lie votes given thereon, it shall be declared adopted, and from and after tho close of
that Communication, shall become a part of the Constitution.
Hmi. 4. No vote upon a proposed amendment shall be taken after the election of
the Grand officers.

with this Constitution; and no Hegulation shall hereafter be adopte<l wl!ich shall be
