REPRESENTATrvE.-The Representative of a Lodge within this State is one who,
being a member thereof, in the event that neither the Master nor either of the Wardell8
can be present at the Grand Lodge, has been elected by the Lodge, at 11 stated meeting, or at a special meeting called for that purpose, by ballot, and by a majority
of the votes present, to represent it at the next Communication. A Lodge without
the State may be represented by a member of any Lodge under this jurisdiction,
elected as before.
VAOA..'!CY.-Vacancies in office, either in a Lodge or in the Grand Lodge, may
occur by death, deprivation, resignation, removal from the jurisdiction, suspension,
or expulsion.
JmusnroTioN.-The jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge iuclndes all Lodges and llfa·
sons within the territorial limits of this State, and all Lodges and their members
without this State, acting under its authority :
The jurisdiction of a Lodge includes all Masons residing nearer to its place of
meeting than to that of any other Lodge within this State, except in towns or cities
where more than one Lodge exists ; in which case, each of such Lodges has separate jurisdiction over its own members, and concurrent jurisdiction over all Masons,
not members of one of such Lodges, who reside in such town or city, or nearer
thereto than to any other place where a Lodge exists.
REGULATION~By a regulation of the Grand Lodge is meant al!y resolution, edict,
, Jaw, or ordinance of any kind whatever, other than the Constitution, which tt may
adopt.
SusPENSION~The suspension of a Lodge is an arrest of its charter and a temporary prohibition to assemble or work as a legal Lodge, until again authorized so to
do by competent authority; and the act suspends all its membel's except those espe·
cially exempted from its effect.
The suspension of the Master of a Lodge is a temporary deprivation of his office,
and prohibits all recognition of him in that capacity, until he be restored by compe·
tent authority.
·
The suspension of a Mason is a temporary deprivation of all his rights and privi·
leges as such, and prohibits all Masons and Lodges from holding any MP.sonic
intercourse, whatever, with him, until he shall be legally restored by the Lodge which
suspended him, or by the Grand Lodge.
ExruLSION.-The expulsion of a Mason is the highest penalty known to the Ma·
sonic law. It is an absolute deprivation of all the rights and privileges of the Order,
and prohibits all Masons and Lodges from holding any Masonic intercourse with him
forever, unless he be restored by the Grand Lodge.
NoTrFIOATJON.-A notification is a call issued by the Secretary, by order of the
Lodge or Master, or by other competent authority as hereinbefore provided, to
attend for some specific purpose at the time and place therein indicated; and it Is
the duty of every Mason to comply with its direction, if he can, without great incon·
venience, do so.
SmL'10Ns.-A summons is an imperative order, issued by the Master, or by other
competent authority as hereinbefore provided, to appear at such time and place as
may therein be designa!.ed. The obligation to obey it is absolute, ruid the penalty
for disobedience shall be expulsion, unless it shall be shown that such disobedience
was unavoidable, or was occasioned by some pressing necessity.
STATED M1mTINGs.-The stated meeting of a Lodge is the one only meeting in
each lunar month at whiclt business may be done, with the exceptions specified in
sec. 2, Art. II, Part HJ. It shall be designated as such in the by-laws of each Lodge,
and no adjourned or called meeting shall ever be considered as a part of such stated
meet.Ing.

GENERAL REG UL.A TIO~S.

I. The practice of dueling being repugnant to the principles of Freemasony, in
nil cases where two brethren resort to this mode of settling their disputes, it shall be
Urn 1lnty of the Lodge or Lodges of which they are members, or within whose juris111111.lon they may reside, forthwith to expel them from all the rights and privileges of
M1LHonry; and no brother who may fall in a dnel shall be buried with Masonic hon-

"''"· [1854.]
2. All bodies purporting to be Masonic Lodges-held in the United States or any
111' t.hcir Territories, within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of any State or Terri-

f.11ry, without authority from such Grand Lodge-and all the members thereof, are de·
11i1Lred illegal. [1854.]
:i. All Lodges within this State, having concurrent jurisdiction with other Lodges,
Mlmll immediately notify such others of all applications for membership or initiation.
11~r.4.]

4. This Grand Lodge, having recognized the principle that no one should be initi·
tLl.<Hl into the mysteries of our Order, except in the Lodge nearest his place of
l'llHldence, (unless by its permission,) and having, by an established regulation, taken
1•11ro to avoid infringing the jurlsffictfonal rights of others, will not tolerate that its
11wn be invaded; and it is therefore ordered that no Lodge, subordinate to the Grand
l.111lge of California, shall admit to membership any person who, being at the time a
l'llHl1lent of this State, ha& received, or claims to have received, the degrees of MaM1111ry from any sourco beyond its jurisdiction, without the proper permission, until
hn Ahall have paid the Lodge to which he applies for membership, the full a.mount
1il11irged by that Lodge for conferring the degrees, less the sum paid by him to
l.llll Lodge in which he received them. (1855 and 1857.)
r.. This Grand Lodge recognizes no degree of Past Master conferred by any an·
t.hol'ity not holden under a legitimate Grand Lodge-acknowledging only the Or<ler
11r that name as it exists in the ceremonies attending the installation of the Master
olcct of a chartered Lodge ; which Order shall be conferred only by a convocation
111' Present or Past Masters, not less than three in nnmber, who havo thus regnlarly
l'<rncived it. [1855.]
n. All Masonic communication between the Lodges and Masons of this jarisdicf.lon and those acknowledging allegiance to the Grand Lodge of Hamburg, is hereby
1'11rbidden, while that body shall continue its unlawful and reprehensible invasion of
lho jurisdictional rights of the Grand Lodge of New York. [1855.]
7. Such standard of revenue shall be continned hereafter as will afford an excess
over the current expenditures of at least one thousand dollars; which excess shall
1u1ch year be set aside, as an accumulating fund, for the future erection of a Masonic
lllLll, and shall not be used for any other purpose. At each Annual Communication,
11 Board of Trustees, three in number, shall be elected, whose duty it shall be judi·
1•lonsly to invest all moneys set aside for such fund, and all moneys accruing from
lhu interest on such investments ; and each member of said Board shall execute and

than the conferring of degrees, with a less number than seven members present.
[1859.]

10. The Grand Secretary is authorized to charge the sum of one dollar, for the
use of the Grand Lodge, for each copy of its printed proceedings for the current
yeo.r, other than the four copies to be sent to each subordinate Lodge, and those required for transmission abroad, for future binding, and for the use of the Grand
Lodge at its next succeeding Annual Communication. [1859.]
11. All Masons, heretofore stricken from the rolls of Lodges within this jurisdiction, for non-payment of dues, who have not been re·instated, are hereby declared
to be suspended, as provided in Sec. 9, Art. m, Part m, of the Constitution. [1859.]
12. The names of Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts shall bo returne:i to the
Grand Lodge for two years only, in either of those degrees, but this shall not affect
their position in their respective Lodges. [186Q, 1862.)
13. In addition to the dues prescribed in the Constitution, there shall be levied
hereafter upon the subordinate J.odges the sum of seventy-five cents for each Master
Mason whose name is borne upon their rolls at the date of the annual returns, which
shall constitute a special fWld to be denominated "The Representative Fund ; " and
it shall be the duty of the several Lodges to pay the said sum at the time and in the
manner directed in the Constitution for the payment of their annual dues. At each
Annual Communication, an auditing committee, to consist of three, shall be appointed by the Grand Master, who shall audit all accounts of represent&tives of Lodges
for their necessary traveling expenses to and from the place of the Communication,
and shall certify the amount due each representative to the Grand Secretary, who
shall thereupon draw his warrant upon the Grand Treasurer therefor ; but no warrant shall issue to more than one representative from any Lodge, nor shall any rep•
resentative receive payment for such traveling e:i:penses whose Lodge shall not have
paid its dues for the current year, or who shall not have been in attendance during
the entire Communication. [1861, 1865.]
14. The appointed Grand Officers and the chairmen of standing committees shall
receive payment for their necessary traveling expenses to and from ea~h Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge, in the same manner as ordered for the representatives of Lodges; but no such officer, chairman, or representative shall receive
such payment in more than one of those capacities, nor shall he receive it unless he
shall have been in attendance at such Communication from the first to the last day
thereof, inclusive, (unless excused by the Grand Lodge,) nor if he shall already have
been paid for such traveling expenses by any other Masonic Grand Body. (1862,
186$, 1864.]

16. The work and lectures presented by tl1e committee appointed for their exam·
lnation and revision, are approved, adopted, and made obligatory upon all Lodges
within this jurisdiction; and any Lodge which shall have had O'pportunity to obtain
instruction therein, and shall neglect or refuse to learn and use the same, shall, upon
representation of that fact to the Grand Master, be liable to the arrest of its charter,
if, in his discretion, he shall think it proper. (1863, 1864.]
IG. Non-affiliated Masons, who are suspended by operation of Sec. 1, Art. II,
Part V, of the Constitution, if they desire to restore themselves, eitl\er by affiliation
or contribution, shall pay a sum equivalent to six months' dues, in addition to the
a.fflliation fee required by the by·laws of the Lodge to which they may apply, or a

Mum of money equal to one dollar per month for all the time during which they have
rflHided within the jurisdiction of the Lodge, unless sickness or inability to pay be
Mhown as the reason for non-affiliation or non-payment. [1864.]
17. ·when it is the intention of any Lodge to take measures to apply to the Grand
Lodge for the restoration of a Mason who has been expelled, it shall be the duty of
the Master thereof to notify the members of his Lodge, as far as possible, of the
time when such proposed action will be had; and to cause to be recorded, in the minutes of the meeting at which such action sliall be had, the fact that such Ilotilication
w11s duly given. [1864.]
18. The person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man; no woman nor
uunuch; freeborn, neither a slave nor the son of a bondwoman; a believer in God
1111d a futnre existence ; of moral conduct ; capable of reading and writing ; not delorme_!l or dismembered, but hale and sound in his physical conformation, having his
right limbs as a man ought to have; and be able to conform literally to what the
Hovcral degrees respectively require of him. [1864.]

I.he jndgmcnt of the subordinate Lodge or whose sentence of suspension has boon

The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge, as follows:BRETHREN OF TRE GRAND LODGI!: OF CALIFORNIA :With steadier aim and strengthened purpose we come again'to counsel together
for the good of our Ancient Craft, and to renew those social and fraternal pledges
which have for ages united us in a persistent will to magnify and enforce the great
tenets of our Fraternity. We have cause for congratulation, as citizens and Masons, In
the general prosperity which has been vouchsafed to us, but there is special obliga·
tion to thank the Omnipotent Grand Master above who bas deemed us worthy to be
crowned with his mercy and loving kindness.
Since our last Annual Communication the material comforts which add to man's
happiness have been signally bestowed upon us. The horn of plenty again pours forth
the rich fruits of peace; the fateful trinity, war, pestilence, and famine, are strangers
to us; and contentment, with placid smile, lightens the countenance of all who ration·
ally appreciate His goodness who has givea us these blessings. But while we are so
kindly favored by a beneficent and seeming partial Providence, let us not permit our
charities to slumber. All lands are not so blessed as ours. The flame of war,
with its attendant troop of woes, which burned so fiercely in our country, was
quenched only to burst forth with equal hea.t and fury upon our brethren beyond
the seas; and with deep sympathy and interest it was natural to turn our hearts
toward them and pray that they too might be gifted with the same fortunate
wisdom and counsel which preserved the unity of our Brotherhood here, and,
clothed in warm humanity, led us through fields of carnage unstained by acts incon·
sistent with our high professions. That Almighty hand which, by His inscrutable will,
was laid in anger upon us and raised in mercy, is again uplifted, and on the bloody
field of Sadowa the same sentiment which animated us shines conspicuously in the
acts of the good COUNT THEODORE STOLBERG, a name to be honored by Masons, who,
with the noble Knights of St. John of Jerusalem, was ever present in the hospitals,
and constant in relieving 11Ulfering and softening the horrors of war.
Neither are all portions of our own land as blessed as this. The desolating track of
armies has left no charred monuments to remind ns of the houselesa and homeless
suiferer; the shock of battle has not scarred our landscape or dotted the fields with

290

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 9,

the lonesome tenements of the dead. We are not so piteously reminded, as have
been our brethren by the Atlantic, of the inevitable result of war-the widow and
the orphan whom it bequeaths as a legacy to ~harit.able hands. Those claims at our
doors, which always appeal so strongly, being relieved, there remains abundant opportunity for those of us who have been thus favored to extend our charities farther,
and draw forth the tears of gratitude where those of sorrow flow.
I believe, from the best information received, that the general condition of our
Society is one of eminent prosperity. The numerol1s instances of recent record by
which the sincerity of our professions have been tested and nobly illustrated, have
done much to strengthen the bond which ever unites us; and hands, lately raised in
wrath, have joined around our common 11.ltars, sinking the pa•t in oblivion. The Grand
Lodges have just reason for conscious pride in the wisdom of their action dnritJg their
perilous day and generation, and may rightfully expect that those who shall HUcceed
us will remember how earnestly and faithfully they strove to preserve, unspotted nnd
unblemished, the integrity of' the ancient charges which they were commi•sioneu to
guard. Free·masonry in America has for a .~econa time borne itself brnvely and
purely through the perils of storm; and when the night which seemed to close nronnd
our horizon looked darkest, and the tempest of passion howled fiercest, its hopeful
votaries gathered closest around its altars.
Looking abroad, we finrl during the year which hns passeu that estrangements
which embarrassed the intercourse of certai11 Grand Ludgcs with each othc1· have
been adjusted, and that cordial and fraternal relations which were temporarily
suspended have been happily renewed. It is with plea>ure that I announce to
you that the alienation between the distinguished Grand Lodges of Virgirtia and
New York, mothers.of many of us here, no longer exists. The ediet of non-intercourse promulgated six years since by the former ·against the latter, on account
of the application of our laws by the latter in the matter of the Philips organization, baa
been withdrawn, and the relation which existed between them in the olden time, with
all its pleasant reminiscences, is restored. Fraternal hands, too, have been uxtended to each other by the Ornnd Lodges of the District ofColumhia antl Virginia, which
gives hope that the wise counsel which has been gracefully and fruitfully exchanged
in the case just alluued to will eventually succeed in ju~tifying the abolition of' the
edict of non·intercourse declared by t.hc latter against the former on acconnt .of the
invasion of her jurisdictional rights. While we may not otl'er officious counsel, we are
permitted to express the hope that the variance of opinion which exists between
them may be speedily settled tipon sonnd and cstabli"lrnd principles of Masonic law.
The history of these things will, doubtless, be fully laid before you by our committee
whose province it is to report snch matters.
Within our own immediate bordcn we have enjoyed our share of prosperity and
success, and true hearts are found watchfully guarding our altars. Naturally, in a
jurisdiction so large and extensive, doubts and difficulties have at times arisen in the
Lodges and in the minds of the officers in regard to their dntie•; but wlien such matters
have been referred to me, a careful examination of the question submitted bus resulted in inspiring stronger confidence in your previous legislntion and the excellent Constitution upon which it is based, and instruction has been given accordingly. Most of

In this connection it maybe proper to say that the organic law, and the legislation
growing from it, has established rules so clear that studious Lodges cannot be at loss
upon the leading questions relating to jurisdictional rights. Twelve months actua.f
residence within the territorial jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, and six months
within that of one of its subordinates next preceding an application, is absolutely
required before a petition for degrees can be received. The power to dispense with'
this requirement does not, in this State, belong to the Grand Master. A Lodge cannot

lawfully pass or raise an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft, upon whom the antbor·

each Lodge within the State, except those located in the cities, which have concur,
rent jurisdiction, extends in every direction to the geographical center between it
and the contiguous Lodges. The air line governs, and not the route of travel. I
recite these rules because I have so applied the laws in special cases which appealed
to the executive authority since the last Communication of the Grand Lodge.
Some of the Masters have sought my advice in regard to a certain regnlation
by which it was intended to define and determine more distinctly the standing of
those troublesome brethren of ours who, though unwilling to submit to the wholesome duty of membership, yet expect, without good reason, to share the same
privileges enjoyed by those who do. The Regulation, No. 16, adopted at our
}'ifteenth Annual Communication, and intended as a guide in such matters, is evi·
dently not understood. The phraseology is vague and uncertain, and should be
reconstructed to express more clearly the legislation designed. The intention,
doubtless, was to promote affiliation and place the Mason who dwells within a sub·
ordinate jurisdiction more than six months without joining a Lodge, or making !ln
effort to do so, in the same category with the member of a Lodge who is suspended
for non-payment of dues; that is, that d11es shall continue to be chargeable to him.
If that was and now is the intention, then I recommend that the law be remodeled
to read as follows :"REGULATION 16. Non-affiliated Masons who are suspended by operation of Sec,
1, Art. II, Part V, of the Constitution, if they desire. to restore themselves by affiliation, shall pay a sum equivalent to six months dues in audition to the affiliation fee
required by the by-laws of th~ Lodge to which they may apply, or, if they desire to
restore themselves by contribution, they shall pay a sum equivalent to the amount
of the regular dues of the Lodge within whose jurisdiction they reside, during the
wl1ole period of such residence, unless sickness or inability to pay be shown as the
reason for non-affiliation or non-payment."
As the printed Regulation now stands, I have held that the unaffiliated Mason,
against whom the law is especially directed, may elect which of the two conditions
he will comply with, and of course he accepts the least stringent.
The subject of uniformity of work has engaged my attention. Although, in a

ance of stlict attention to and compliance with the Regulations in this respect.

It will be seen that during two years past the number of dispensations issued for
the establishment of new Lodges has been considerably leas than during any like pe·
rlod of time since the organization of this Grand Lodge; and it might seem from this
that the craft in this jurisdiction is not so prosperous, so far at least as increase in
numbers is concerned, as it has been In former years. Such a conclusion, however,
would be a mistaken one. Though the growth of Lodges has been less exuberant,
and a number of those first planted have disappeared, the increase in the number of
members of Lodges during the past ten years has been constant nnd comparatively
steaily, except as shown in the tables of last year, when the diminution was caused
by the withdrawal of the eight Nevada Lodges, comprising a membership of more
than four hundred. In the earlier days, in almost every little mining camp, 11 number
of Masons could be found, and forthwith a Lodge was prayed for and established.
After a season, more or less brief, the "gulch" wa.s worked out, and so also was the
liodge. The charter was surrendered and the brethren departed for other "diggings,"
but almost always to form some new Lodge, or affiliate with one already organized.
The growth of Lodges is now a more healthy one. Our population is more fixed and
permanent, and though neither it nor onr membership increases with such propor·
tionate rapidity aR was exhibited in the first few years of gold hunting immigration,
there is every reason to be satisfied with our present condition and with our prospects for the future. It ill gratifying, too, to know that. one cause.fo~ such dimi~ution
of increase is found in the evident greater care taken Ill the adm1asiou of candidates,
as our statistics show that during the last ten years about ono fourth of all the appli·
cants for degrees have been rejected.
•
The numbers upon our registry of chartered Lodges have now reached to one
hundred and seventy-six. Of these, one hundred and forty-two, excluding the one
whose dissolution has just been reported, still exist under our jurisdiction; and, of
the remaining thirty-four, ten have been transferred to Oregon and Nevada, twenty·
one have voluntarily surrendered their charters, and three have ~uf.fered the revoca·
tion of those instruments by the Grand Lodge. There are, besides, five Lodges acting.
under dispe1.sations, making in all one hundred and forty-seven Lodges at present
in active existence under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, one of wbich is in the
Territory of Arizona, and another in the Kingdom of the Hawaiian Islands.

that, on this score, there has been any delinquency during the past year. To enable
the writer to say this, however, it was necessary to remind several Lodges which,
until very recently, had neglected to discharge this duty, that it was a neceSS1Lry one.

But one case of the removal of a Lodge from the place of meeting named in ita.
charter has occurred during the past year. The members of Eel .River Lodge, No.
147, at Hydesville, in Humboldt County, being unanimously desirous to meet thereafter at Rohnerville, in the same county, and having taken the measures made nece8'
sary by our Jaws, before application to the Grand Master, on the twenty-second day:
of December last received from him the requisite permission tor such removal;
which, having been entered upon the record book of that J,odge, is now submitted.
A resolution of the Grand Lodge, adopted in November, 1851, directed that an
impression of the seal of each subordinate Lodge should be deposited in the offiee,of
the Grand Secretary, for preservation and reference ; and it has been found that the
regulation was a useful one, as In several cases, in the interior towns, w:here Lodges
have Jost all their property by fire, their seals included, the impressjons in this offioe
served to perpetuate the originals in the engraving of new ones. But many of the
earlier Lodges had neglected to make such deposit; and those which did comply with
the regulation had the impressions taken in wax,or simply upon paper, most of which
have become broken up or obliterated. Since the undersigned has occupied the of.•
fice of Grand Secretary, the greater portion of the seals of Lodges established during that period have been procured through him, and in all such cases counter·dies on
lead have been preserved. Deeming it desirable to have impressions of all the Lodge
seals taken in this durable form, a request was recently transmitted by him to those
Lodges- some sixty or seventy in number - whose seals were not thus represented
here, to forward them to this office, in order that such impressions might be pre·
served. Nearly all the Lodges have already complied with the request, and It is not
doubted that the co!lection will soon be complete. This will involve some expense
to the Grand Lodge for express charges, as it was not thought proper to let the
Lodges be chargeable therewith; but it will not be of great amount, and it is hopild
that the action of the undersigned will meet with approbation.
Sundry proposed amendments to the by-laws of chartered Lodges-twenty-two in
number-have been received dnring the year. Fourteen of these change the rates ot
fees or dues; seven alter the days of stated meetings; and one amends the system of
ballotting, by proposing one ballot for the three degrees, instead of a separate one for
er.ch, as was practiced in that I..odge theretofore. All have been approved by the
Grand Master, as they involved only such changes as, with his sanction, are permitt.
ed by our laws until the succeeding Annual Communication; and they are now presented, in accordance with those Jaws, for final action by the Grand Lodge, as an
also the by-laws of the five Lodges now existing under disperuiation. .

The Constitution directs the Grand Secretary " to report, at each Annual Commn·
nication, all unfinished business of the Grand Lodge." During several yefl,rs past, it
has not been the custom of this body to leave much, if 11on7, real " business" In that
state; but as the following matters were certainly" unfl.nished" at the elose of the
last Annual Meeting, they are now here noted:.F'irst-The Trustees of the Masonic Hall Fund, with two other,lmembers of the
Grand Lodge, were instructed, at the last Commnnication "to make inquiries into the
affairs of the Masonic Hall AS80ciation of San Francisco." (See pages 91 and 100,
proceedings of 1865.) No inquiries have been made by those brethren, so far as the
undersigned is informed; but he has the pleasure of submitting herewith a late report
of a committee of stockholders in that association, which, as the committee was com·
posed of an influential representative from each of the Masoaic bodies in this city
owning stock therein-twelve In number-with three of the largest Individual stock·
holders, it is hoped will prove satisfactory to the brother who sought the information.
Seoond. The Grand Secretary wus " instructed to prepare and publish in the pro·
ceedings of the present year, (1865,) a form for the proper keeplag of Lodge
records." See page 121, proceedings of 1865. This was not then done for the
reason that the creditable preparation of such a guide for the Lodges, which should
illustrate the manner of keeping a recqrd·book, from the ·preliminary meeting or
meetings of brethren who wish to establi8h a Lodge, through the various stages of
obtaining a dispensation, and subsequently a charter, to the period of its dissolution,
with the many necessary formulas for a proper entry of the history of the work and
of the manifold varieties of business which might be transacted by a Lodge, required
more time than could be given without an unreasonable and unnecessary delay of
the publication of the proceedings of that year. Moreover, although the under·
signed gratefully appreciated the compliment bestowed upon him by the Grand
Lodge, in thus giviag him authority to promulgate snch a form, it appeared to him
best that a publication of that kind, apparently intended to be mandatory upon the
Lodges, should first be submitted to that body for its inspection and approval, so
that, if approved, it might carry with it tne authority with which i't was probably
Intended to be invested- For these reasons, which it is hoped will be deemed sufficient, the preparation of the paper was delayed; and, though presented now, it is
still deemed incomplete and needing many additional suggestions.
Third. The elective ofllcers of the Grand Lodge were appointed a committee" to
procure a suitable testimonial for presentation to Past Grand Master WILLIAM C.
BELCHER," at the present Communication, "as an evidence of !ti just appreciation
of the able, zealous, and faithful manner in which the duties of the Grand Mastership" had been performed by him during more than three years of service. That
duty has been fulfilled, and the manner of its performance will, in due season,
doubtless, be presented to you by the Grand Master •
li'ourth. The Grand Secretary was imtructed to procure a portrait of Past Grand
Master BELOilllR, to be hung in one of the offices of the Grand Lodge. Bro.
BELCHEB's non-residence in this city, and sickness in the family of the artist em·
ployed, have thus far prevented the complete fultlllment of this duty; but the
Instruction will be carried into elfect at the earliest moment possible.

It is a source of much gratification to be enabled to announce that, during the
past year, the communication with our brethren of the South, so long, and for so
painful a cause, Interrupted, has been resumed, and that, as in detail will be seen in
the Report on Correspondence, the back proceedings of most of the Southern Grand
Lodges have been received. But there are yet some deficiencies in our files of the
transactions of these and other Grand Lodges which the writer would gladly see
supplied ; and, for the purpose of respectfully calling the attention of his brother
Grand Secretaries to his wish, the following statement is given:From Arkansas we miss the proceedings of 1861. From Delaware we have nothing
since 1864. From Florida are missing the transactions of 1862antl1863. Prom Georgia
we have not received those of 1862, 1863, and 1864. From Illinois nothing has reach·
ed us since 1864. From Minn.esota we have nothing since l8fl, except the pro·
ceedings of 1863. From Mississippi nothing later than 1861. From Sonth Carolina.
nothing since 1859. And from Tennessee we miss the transactioll.fl of 1861 and 1862.
It ls proper to say that, in answer to letters upon the subject, information has been
received from several Grand Secretaries and other Grand Officers, that, in some of the
cases above named, the non.appearance of the expected publications was caused
either by a failure to hold the Annual Communications, or to print their proceedings
when held; and in these instances, the communications have contained kindly promises that the deficiencies shall be remedied so far and as soon as possible.

The Committee on Correspondence present the following report, reviewing the
proceedings of sister Grand Lodges so far as received. We have the pleasure of
welcoming most of our former correspondents in the southern part of the Union,
11nd we greet them with glad hearts, for that the hindering cause is removed. War
has ceased its desolating and devastating reign in our native land, and the United
Htates of America, undivided and indivisible, begin a new era in their history. The
differences of opinion engendered during years of strife, must not be permitted to
onter our sacred Masonic retreats, to mar the harmony and disturb the peace of the
llraternity. We rejoice to know that this is the almost universally-expressed view of
the Brotherhood, as given utteranee to in the volumes we have perused; and especially is this the case among the Grand Lodges of the northern States-Grand Masters
11nd Committees on eorrespondence vying with each other in expressions of friend·
llness and earnest desire that all will " let the dead past bury its dead," and act,
and work, and strive in the " living present." Nor are onr southern brethren
hehind in expressions of acquiescence in the present state of affairs .. This spirit
11nimating all parties, we grow strong in hope that the cement of brotherly love and
111fection will be so spread by the Master Workmen among us with the silver trowel
of kindly speech, that the whole body of the F'raternity, fitly joined and compacted
hy that which every part supplieth, shall grow into a Grand Living Temple, whose
hcautiful proportions will have to every beholder more the appearance of being the
work of the t'lupreme Architect of the Universe than of the heart and mind of man.

ALABAMA.

The proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Alabama for the years 1862-63-64-65,
have come to our pouession, and we are glad to welcome again to our list this sister,
and hail the evidence afforded by the reception of these and other proceedings from.
soutliern Grand Lodges, that the civil war is over, with great plea.sure. We are
sorry, however, to find that politics were permitted to lntrnde into the addresses and
reports of the Grand Officers and committees, and that they are not exempt from the
wrong they charge against their northern brethren. We excuse this neither in the
one or the other, and regret that any Mason in high place, in either section, should
have pernrltted himself to be so far carried away by the circumstances of the hour
as to use expressions which, however well they may have been in the mouth of a
citizen in an assemblage of citizens, were unbecoming in the mouth of a Mason, and
within the sacred precincts of a Grand Lodge.
The forty-second Annual Communication was held in the City of Montgomery,
commencing on the first day of December, 1862. The ]If.·. W.-. WM. II. Noams,
Grand Master, presided, and the R.·. W.·. DAN.IEL SAYRE was Grand Secretary. The
Grand Master's Address, with the exception of the expressions mentioned above, is
a well considered pa.per. He mentions in fitting terms the decease of the M.-. W.-.
STEPHEN F. HALE, Pa.st Grand Master, and mourns over the diminished attendance
at the Grand Lodge, owing to the vicissitudes of a state of war. He rendered a
number of decisions, some of which were concurred in aud some reversed by the
Grand Lodge. He decided, for instance, that in the absence of the Master and
Wardens, a Past Master might take the Ea.st, open the Lodge, and transact business.
The Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence reported against the decision, and held
that a Past Master had no authority, and could not a.ct unless one of the Wardens
was present and congregated the Lodge. We esteem this good law; hut the same
committee decided another point in a manner which we hold in less esteem, and
which tlley would be as ready to denounce in a northern committee as any one. The
question was submitted whether a. Mason, deserting to the enemy, and being a citizen of Alabama, could be tried and punished as for a Masonic offense. The com·
mittee present an elaborate report, arguing that ordinarily _it would not be an offense
punishable as a Masonic misdemeanor ; but, under the circumstances of the existing
war, it was a high crime, and punishable by the Lodge as such. The very same
Grand Lodge which endorses this opinion, in 1865 held it a grave wrong for any
Lodge in the United States to have expelled a Mason for joining the Confederate
ranks, although his State refused to secede. Circumstances apparently alter casesa.nd we say here distinctly that we have found in our perusal of the proceedings of
the Grand Lodges of the northern States, no such harsh and unbrotherly language,
no such declarations of non-intercourse with the southern Masons, ae we have read
in the proceedings under review, and quoted from other jurisdictions by their Committee on Correspondence. We a.re sorry in our very heart of hearts that truth
compels us to say this. We had fondly cherished the hope that nothing of the kind
would have been found ; but in all the proceedings of this State prior to the Commu·

1866.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

307

nlcation of 1865, (which was held after the rebellion had been subdued,) the allusions
to the North, and even to northern brethren and Grand Lodges, are of the harshest
und most unkindly character. We should have refrained from saying a single word
ILbout this but for the fact that the Grand Lodges and Fraternity in the North are
called to account for this thing, and we desire that both sides be fairly and plainly
stated. Charges are made by the Grand Secretary, which a.re not only out of pl 11 ce
ln a document of the kind, even if true, but, being as they l'l'ere and are utterly and
wholly void of truth, were unfit to be spoken even on the hustings. The same thing
may be said of the Report on Correspondence. We have no disposition to take the
offensive, hut we could not do less than defend our brethren of the North, and strive
to open the eyes of those brethren of Alabama. to their own derelictions, which
should lrnve had the effect, when called to mind, to mitigate their blame of those in
the North who had done only as they themselves did.
The Grand Master and Grand Secretary were hoth reelected.

The forty-fifth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of the State of
Alabama was held in the City of Montgomery, commencing on the fourth day of
December, 1865-the ,lf.·. W.·. WM. C. PENNICK, Grand Master, presiding, and the
R.·. w.·.DANI!".L SAYRE being Grand Secretary.
The Grand Master, in his Address, notices the political status of atrairs-the rise
and fall of governments-the devastations of war-the fleeing away of riches-the
overthrow of their peculiar institution-and admonishes the brethren that, as good
Masons, they should submit themselves to the powers that be. He reiterates the
ancient charge that in the State a Mason is to be a quiet and peaceable citizen, true
to his government and just to his country ; that he is not to countenance disloyalty
or rebellion, but patiently submit to legal authority, and conform with cheerfulness
to the government of the country in which he lives. He tells us that, although Ma·
sonry, according to the ancient charges, has ever been injured by war, and acknowledges that the world's history might be brought to witness the truth of the declara.tion ; yet, if there has ever been an e:s:ception to the rule, the civil wa.r in our country
was that exception. Masonry in his jurisdiction was a triumph, a.s many having
been initia.ted, passed, and raised during the year as in a.ny one preceding it. He
laments, however, that many had come into the Fraternity through interested motives, and now that the war is ended, having no further use~or the institution, will
dimit, and remain on the outside. And this leads him to present the subject of nonaffiliated Masons. This class, the Grand Master says, is " numerous and increasing; they claim much, receive much, aud do little or nothing.'' He then goes on to
argue that they are "expatriated Masons "-drones in the Masonic hive-and recommends that those who ha.ve remained non-affiliated for two years should be notified by the Lodge within whose jurisdiction they live, that if they do not become
members of some regular J,odge within twelve months they shall be indefinitely suspended from all the rights, privileges, and benefits of }fasonry-to be restored only
by petition. He r.ecommends an amendment to the Constitution in regard to atlilia.·
tions, and ~nother substituting the word " United," for the word" Confederate;" and
the Committee to whom the matters were referred, reported adversely in regard to
the first, a.nd, as to the other, that the word " Corifedlrrate" had never been legally

1866.]

Grand Lodge of Odlifyrnia.

"ttbstituted for " United," and that the Secretary should restore the proper phraseology, wherever necessary.
The Grand Master reports that, prior to the occupation of Montgomery by the
Federal troops, he removed some of the property of the Grand Lodge lest it might
lJe destroyed, and would have removed all had he been able ; but he had found that
It was an unnecessary precaution, as nothing was disturbed. He further records the
Jl<lelity of a b'rother in the Federal army, who, finding in the possession of a comrade, not a Mason, the jewels of a Lodge, purchased them and left them with a brother at Montgomery, to be restored to the Lodge whose hall had been destroyed
and p!llaged. These instances will tend very greatly to restore good feeling; and if
we will all, North and South, dwell upon these, rather than those calculated to irritate
and inflame, it will be the means of bringing hack once more the old friendships, and
promote that harmony in the Fraternity and the State, which wlll make us strong for
good.
A committee of investigation in a. Lodge had reported: "We, the committee,
recommend that Mr. A. and Mr. B. be balloted for." The Master refused to receive
the report, as being insufficient ; an<l the brethren desiring to submit the matter to
the Grand Master, it was so done, and he sustained the ruling of the Master. Committees are too apt to shirk their duties in just this style, and if every Master would
take the course of our brother in Alabama, it would come to pass, in a very short
time, that the reports of committees would give the information t.o obtain which they
are appointecl.
The Grand Master was applied to, to know whether a Mason expelled in one jurisdiction, coulil be alllllated by a Lodge in his jurisdiction ; and he replied, of course,
that he could not-that the consent of the jurisdiction which expelled him must first
be obtained.
this connection, however, he mentions tliat there are numerous
cases of MasoM who have been expelled by their Lodges for joining the Confederate
service, a.nd he recommends the Grand J,odge to take some action in order to bring
the matter before the Grand Lodges of the jurisdictions where these expulsions took
place; and, by remonstrance or otherwise, induce them to review the cases, and do
justice to the injured brethren. He decided that persons made in Army Lodges
mi~ht affiliate without <limits, but that others must obtain proper evidence of Masonic
standing from their Lodges. Several dispensations were granted to Lodges, which
had lost charters and other property by the raids of .Federal soldiers, empowering
them to continue to work. He decided tha.t those who had lost an arm or a leg can
not be initiated, and stated that. lie had refused all a.pplications for dispensations to
confer degrees without time. We a.re glad to note the growing opinion among the
Grand Masters that tills d!Apensing power was granted to them, not for the benefit of
profanes, or of any individuals, but only for the good of the Fraternity. Certain
parties, hailing from another jurisdiction, deRired to be made Masons in Alaba.ma,
but the law of that State required the Lodge to which they. applied to ascertain
whether tbey had ever been refused admission by the Lodge nearest which they bad
before resided, and whether they knew of any just cause why they should not be
made Masons, and forbade any J,odge to make residents of other jurisdictions without this prior inquiry and proper reply. Upon application to him, the Grand Ma.ster
decided that the state of war rendering communication impossible, the applicants
might be admitted, if otheqvise worthy, without the inquiry. The committee, however, to whom the matter was referred, decided, and the Grand J,odge concurred,
that a state of war did not annul their Constitution, and that applica.nts must wait
until communication was re-opened. The matter of a Grand Lodge Hall was pre·
sented in the Address, a.nd subsequently referred to a committee.
The Report of the Grand Secretary shows tha.t the Fraternity is measurably prosperous. He rejoices over the return of peace, and speaks of the destruction of the
"monuments of the peculiar institution, as well as many evidences of our Southern

there being a fnll representation of' officers and members of the Grand Lodge.
The Address of the Grand Master notices that the " perfect period of seven years"
had passed since the Grand Lodge assembled in Annual Commnnicatlon in that hall.
Many who had tben met with them had gone from the Imperfect Lodge, summoned
by the wise Master Builder. He speaks of it as a day of comparatively small things
as the Grand Lodge then numbered but one hundred Lodges-their financial condl:
tion was by no means commensurate with their dignity as a Grand Body-their work
was unsatisfoctory--and but few sister Grand Lodges. had acknowledged them. Now
they had more than one hnndred and ~eventy Lodges, and the other Items were all
in an improved condition. During the year he liad granted ten dispensations for new
Lodges, but l1ad becr1 careful to issne no dispensation until satisfied of the compe·
tency of the propel' officers. Two applications for dispensation had been refused, be·
cause in one case it would havo interfered with an existing Lodge, and in the other
the Master nominated was utterly unfit to rule hls Lodge or confer degrees. He

Grand Lodge with the importance of taking steps to meet the requirements of the
Craft in this respect. He decided several points of law submitted. to him-among
others, that a llfaster, even jf willing to do so, has I)O power to resign. We may
have occasion, in tlie course of our report, to give our reasons for dltfering with our

man, and one who had lost a limb, could not be admitted. We are glad that the feeling is becoming stronger on this point, and that the utterances of Grand Masters and
Grand Lodges are becoming more definite and decided. He regarded with astonishment the application of a Lodge for leave to install its offioers in public. He refused
the application, he says, "of course." A number of local matters are treated of,.
and, throughout, the address is one well worthy of perusal.

Our brother of Connecticut sides with Wasl1ington Territory in the jurisdictionaJ
controversy with Oregon. We have heretofore avoided giving our own opinion,
but we may as well say here as any where, that if the position of Grand !\faster
REED is true and just, then there can never be a Grand Lodge of the Territory of
Idaho,for we, as Grand Lodges, acknowledge that where one sovereign Grand Lodge ,
has acquired exclusive jurisdiction, it is not competent for another Grand Lodge to
be formed within her limits. If the change of civil jurisdiction does not determine
the Lodge jurisdiction, then it never can be determined. If the e1·ection of that pa.rt
of Washington Tenitory, which now composes Idaho, into a separate territorial gov·
ernment, did not di1•e11t the Grand Lodge of Washington of exclusive Masonic jurisdiction, and open it to all Grand Lodges, then, it being still within the exclusive &fa·.
sonic jurisdiction of a sovereign Masonic Body, a Grand Lodge of Idaho can never
be established without infringing upon that exclusive jurisdiction; yet there is not
11 Grand Lodge in the United States that would hesitate a moment to recognize a duly
constituted Grand Lodge in the Territory of Idaho. Washington herself t>cknowl·
edges that such a Grand Lodge could be formed, and would divest her·ofher claimed
autlrnrity and exclusive jurisdiction; yet she would not admit that a Grand Lodge
could be formed within Washington Territory as now constituted and bounded, or
that,.irf formed, it would divest her of any of her rights over that Territory. We es·
teem the claim of Grand !\faster REED wholly unfounded, while we admit and com·
mend most highly the spirit of courtesy in which all the correspondence has been
carried on. Bro. PAUL himself, in reviewing the action of Virginia in l'egard to the .
formation of the Grand Lodge of West Virginia, states the rule which mn•t be appli•
cable-" the boundaries of a State being definitely given and decided upon, fixes the,
Masonic jurisdiction "-and" Lodges within those boundaries have a right to organ·r'
ize for themselves a Grand Lodge." Now it seems to us that if the Grand Lodge of 1,
Virginia had such exclusive control of the territory, now within tl1e boundaries ot/
the State of West Virginia, as to render it uumasonic for any other Grand Lodge, ~f
ter the determining of those boundaries, to charter Lodges within those bounds, .
then it.was incompetent for the Lodges to form a Grand Lodge-just as incompe·/
tent as though the boundaries of Virginia hud never been changed-just as improp·~,
er as it was for the brethren to form another Grand Lodge within tlie bounds and:
limits of the State of New York, wbile there existed a Sovereign Grand Lodge la.,'
that State. It is the action of the civil power altering and changing, enlarging or'
diminishing, the territorial limits, which determines the jurisdiction .of Gr&n4
Lodges; and to this we must conform, or inextricable confusion will ensue.

from whose jurisdiction he hailed. There was no report from the Conimittee on

We trust the M:. w,., brother of Iowa will turn his attention to the work of editing
an edition of Shakspeare, for the benefit of American youth; as in such a work he
will find a better field for his poetical powers than is afforded by the limits and
proper subjects of a Masonic address. The first fj.ve pages of the Address would
make a very fair spread-eagle Fourth of July speech, but to our mind is wholly out
of place in the Ad<lress of a Grand Master to his brethren of the Grand Lodge. It i.s
fit and proper for Masons to exhibit their love of country, and there are times and
places for so doing. A subordinate or Grand Lodge is not such a place. That this is
so of a subordinate Lodge, Bro. GUILBERT himself admits ; and his argument to
show that what is not allowable in the subordinate Lodge, is "very meet and
proper" in the Grand Lodge, is to our mind wholly inconclusive.
Six dispensations to open new Lodges were granted, and one refused. A Grand
Representative had been appointed near the Grand Lodge of Maine ; the purchase
of the Grand Secretary's library is recommended; the delinquency of a large number of deputy custodians, in respect of making reports, is reprehended; the dissemination of the work had been more extended than ever before ; and allusion is made
to the rapid increase of the l~rnternity in the country and in Iowa-" nine hundred
Masonic births" having transpired in Iowa alone .during the year 1864, and an 41creased number during the year ending at that Communication. The Grand Master
thinks that those made in army Lodges need to be sealed with the seal of the Lodge,
(if so be such institutions have any such thing as a seal,) in order that they may have
some attestation of their claim to Masonic recognition. He deprecates the rapid
increase of membership and Lodges, and fears the popularization of the Fraternity;
he had received many, but had uniformly refused all, applications for dispensations to
make Masons of those who were "not whole, as men ought to be ;" and calls attention to the fact that a profane, a citizen of Iowa, temporarily within the jurisdiction
of a Lodge in Illinois, was made a Mason therein although minus bis right arm-and
this by special dispensation from the Grand Master of lllinois. We shall be very
glad when we can record the fact that we have not found in any of the proceedings
of Grand Lodges, any of these complaints of invasion of jurisdiction, and these violations, as we esteem them, of the ancient landmarks. We do not use this term now
or ever with reference to anything that properly comes within the purview of the
legitimate local regulations of each Grand Lodge ; but we do esteem the requirement of perfection in limbs a landmark, the disregard of which amounts to an innovation on the body of Masonry-which we have all admitted is not in the power of
any to make. Another case of invasion alluded to by Bro. GUILBERT, he says, in a
note, is satisfactorily explained; the question of a single ballot for the three i degrees
is ably discussed, and the conclusion arrived at that there should be but the one ballot, and that the vote on the question of proficiency and advancement should be by
the uplifted hand. If the Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft has, since his admission, been guilty of unmasonic conduct, the view of Bro. GUILBEIIT is that charges
should be preferred against him and an investigation had. We cordially assent to
these views, and in this jurisdiction the practice conforms substantially to them.
The schools of instruction, during the year, are said to have been productive of
great benefit. The death of the Grand Secretary of Indiana is properly alluded to,
as is also that of the venerable and Rev. Bro. CYltrL pgARL, of the Grand Lodge of
Maine. Appended to the address is a Jong letter to the Lodges, which the Grand
Master calls an" Encyclical Letter," containing much good advice to his subordinates, and designed to take the place of a general personal visitation. There are

of them relate to matters local to the jurisdiction; and some have, among us, been

and if received, must" be re-ol!ligated to the performance of every Masonic duty."
If this is the decision under the Constitution of Iowa, we have nothing to say;

all alike, we simply remark that we do not so understand it. The practice of this

finish its work, the candidate has the right to elect. as to which Lodge he will become
connected with, and that signing the By-Laws of the Lodge which raised him was
evidence of his choice of membership in that Lodge. It has been decided in our
jurisdiction that a person is a member of that Lodge in which he receives the degree
of Master Mason, unless the work is done by one Lodge as a favor to, and on be·
half of, another; and in the latter case he becomes a member of the Lodge by which
he was elected and for which the work was done-the Lodge doing the work acting
simply as an agent. He decided that Wardens need not be Past Masters, and there
is little doubt of the correctness of that decision. Our own view is, that the notion
of making a newly-elected Master a Past Master, until he has served a term in office,
is an absurdity. It appears to be a generally received opinion, that either Warden
is competent to preside and confer degrees, without passing through the unnecessary
ceremonies of the Past Master degree ; and if they are so, why need the Master elect
be subjected to this nonsensical routine? He decided that. a vote to recei'Ve a petition must be unanimous; and that if one votes against its reception it must be returned to the petitioner. understand the distinction which the committee make. When a decision is reversed
and the case sent back for new trial, we suppose the case and the parties resume
the status they had before any trial; and if after new trial the accused be acquitted,
he certainly ought not to be considered out of the Lodge. Upon what other grounds
can or will a decision he reversed than that the trial was irregular and illegal, or
that the evidence was not sufficient to convict? If the trial was irregular and illegal
from want of adherence to proper form, the judgment of the appellate body would
be a reversal of the decision under it, and a remanding of the cause for new trial.
If reversal was had because the evidence did not sustain the charge or show the
cominission of a Masonic crime, then the judgment of' reversal would amount to an
acquittal; and the accused should by the judgment of reversal be as though never
accused. They decide that a Mason, expelled by his Lodge, but restored by the
Grand Lod"c mav use the proceedings in restoration as in lieu of a dimit to accom·
pany l1is pc~itlon for affiliation. They also decide that no duly elected and installed
officer can resign. He must serve out his term, but if he removes, dies, is expelled
or suspended, 11is place must be filled pro tempore by appointment, unless it be the
Master, and tlten the Senior Warden succeeds, &c. This we snniose is tpe general
opinion, but we can not for the life of us sec the point to be gained by asserting it.
Why not, with just as much reason, insist that when a Mason has accepted an ottlce
and been installed therein he shall not remove from the place until his time expires?
Why keep an office unfilled, or filled by an unwilling occupant, instead of declaring it
vacant and providing for its being filled by some one who will perform its functions?
Can a man see sulliciently far into the future to guard against the contingencies that
may arise on the morrow? Suppose he accepts in full faith ant! with c¥ery expect·
ation of' being able to fulfill the duties of Master of a Lodge, and is installed to·day,
and to-morrow is compelled, by circumstances he could not foresee or control, to re·
move from the jurisdiction? Why must the office most important to the Lodge remain unfilled by a pcrm:ment occupant for the whole year on the punctillio of nonresignation? We esteem this doctrine equally a:bsurd and unreasonable, let the cir·
eumstanccs be what they may which causes a brother to wisl1 to resign an ofllce.
He is the best judge of' his own business, and he should not be held to the perform·
ance of engagemeots which a change in circum,;tances placerl it out of his power to
keep; nor should the Lodge, it seems to us, be uuoffieercd merely for the sake of
holding to an idea, the reason for which does not exist.

cepting it. We unhesitatingly answer yes, as readily as from those assumed voluntarily when we became a member of the Fraternity. The argument drawn from his
promise, if he be Master, to transmit the charter to his successor, to our mind is of
no force; does he not do so, when handing it to his Senior Warden? Is he not the
proper successor of the Master? Can you prevent the Master removing from the
jurisdiction? And if not, shall he carry the charter along with him and keep it in his
possession in order that he may have it to transfer to his successor at the next annual election? No one would expect any such thing. Yet, to justify this absurdity,
does the rigid and unbending adherence to the non-resignation doctrine necessarily
lead. If he resigns, as in our jurisdiction he may, the Senior Warden becomes his
successor, and to him he transmits the charter; and the Lodge is just as legally held,
and the work just as well done, as if he were present-for Lodges are compelled to
see that they select brethren as Wardens who shall be competent to fill the Master's
chair in case he be taken away by any cause.
Our proceedings of 1865 are but briefly noticed, from the fact that they were received after the conclusion of the report. Grand Master BJCLCHER is complimented upon
his address, as heing in his usual powerful style. Bro. HonNER alludes to the rejection
of the report of the Committee on Jurisprudence, in regard to the right of the accuser to counsel, as an interesting decision relative to Masonic law. If the brother
will look again at the report of the Committee he will see that it was simply a construction of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of California ; and, as the writer of
that report, we have never ceased to wonder at the action of the Grand Lodge in
determining that the Constitution means what it plainly does not mean at all. That
the Constitution might have been amended so as to meet the case is plain; but to say
it did mean, by a resolution which its own provision and the rules of interpretation
say it could not mean, is to make it an instrument of no value, and to throw a cloud
over it that was not necessary. We have no objection to the accuser having counsel, but we do object to being placed in a false position by our Grand Lodge. As
one of its committees we had notjling to do with our own wishes, but with the simple
performance of our duty ; and the duty committed to us, was the construction to be
put upon a certain clause in our Constitution.
The Louisiana Committee evidently do not think well of the action of the Grand
Lodge of the Disll'ict of Columbia in establishing the Lodge at Alexandria; they are
courteously severe upon Ilro. Gun.BERT of Iowa, and his peculiar style of address;
and unite with the Illinois Committee in their condemnation of the mode of speech
used by the distinguished brother in his address of 1864. They do not seem to have
any idea of the possibility of attaining uniformity of work, and commend the Grand
Lodge of Nevada for the re&olution passed in October, 1865, opening the door for
every one to work as he pleased. The action of Missouri, in relation to Masons
made in military Lodges, is condemned as too sweeping in its reach, or as not sufficiently discriminating. It is true, as the committee say, that the initiate is not to
blame. The Lodge holds itself out as regular and justly authorized to work; but so
do all clandestine Lodges; and yet, we require that profanes innocently made in
such shall be J1ealed before we hold Masonic intercourse with them; and each Grand
Lodge must be the judge of the rule by which these Military Lodges shall be meas·
ured, and their work tested. In reviewing the proceedings of Michigan, the committee express the opinion that L~dges under dispensation ought not to affiliate,
withont express permission of the Grand Master; by which they mean, we suppose,
that power to do so shall be granted in the dispensation issued by the Grand Master,
and they certainly have no power and can exercise none not expressly granted in
the instrument calling them into being. The proceedings of New York receive from
this committee, aA from all others, the highest commendation. They agree with the
committee of that jurisdiction, in their comment upon the new regulation of Indiana
allowing a Lodge to try its own Master, and in their conclusion as to West Virginia,

The (l.ecisions of Grand Master BELCHER at that Communication are approved, and the writer does not think there is much difference be·

the election of Master to those who have served as Warden. Bro. WROTH and Bro.
DimIDJOND have e. quiet little talk on the matter of receiving one, whose Lodge is
extinct, without a dirnit. One says he must produce the best evidence he can of the .
extinction of his Lodge, and the other insists that the best evidence is the certificate · ·
of the Grand Lodge under whose jurisdiction the Lodge Jived and died. Bro. WROTH
does not approve of making Masons of men without arms or legs, and agrees with
us, that such loss, even after initiating, debars from advancement. From his review
of Nevada we learn that the regulation which Bro. HOPKINS excepted to, in regard
to requiring of visitors 11 certificate from a Grand J.,udge, was repealed. He thinks
North Carolina was hasty in regard to the supposed invasion of their territory by the
Grand Lodge of New York. We say what we have to say in our review of North
Carolina, and agree with the committee of Maine in condemnation of the spirit and
words of the brethren of the old North Stat.e. The Grand Lodge of Maryland had
established a Lodge at Fortress Monroe, but as soon as communication was opened
witb the Grand Lodge of Virginia, she withdrew her autl1ority, and requested"the
latter Grand Lodge to take charge of the Lodge. That Grand Lodge agreed to do so,
and resolved to grant it a charter, provided tltat those who had received the degrees in that Lodge should be healed. Bro. WROTH does not like this any better than
the brethren of the District of Columbia liked the provision for healing the Masons
made in Union Lodge. The Grand Lodge of the Old Dominion is quite free with her
healing appliances, and it might not be inappropriate to quote a somewhat ancient .
proverb to her, to wit: "Physician, heal thyself." The brethren of Maryland and
the J;'ederal District repudiate the idea that their work was so imperfect and sickly
as to need healing, before being allowe~ to affiliate and hold intercourse with the un·
sullied brethren of Virginia. We ourselves.incline to the opinion that in this matter
the venerable Virgin is rather prudish.
MASSACHUSETTS,
The Grand Lodge of this State holds Quarterly Communications, the records of
which from March to December, 18G:i, including the Annual Communication and the
Stated Meeting for installation, are before us.
Nothing of any general interest or importance to the Craft has been observed by
us in a careful perusal of the proceedings, till the Communication of September, in
which we find a letter from one of the Lodges in Massachusetts to one in tho State
of Georgia, returning through the Grand Lodge, its charter and other property which
had been found by a brother, a sailor in the United States service, and placed with
it for safe keeping until they could be retorned. The letter expresses, in well
chosen words, tlie kindly feeling of the Fraternity North toward their brethren of the
South, and we give place to the following extracts:

The Address of the _Grand Master is a finished paper of its kind. A full tribute is
paid to.Masonry, and due notice iR given to those who have plotted against the peace
of the institution. Speaking of attempts to change and reform it, on the plea of the
progressive character of the age, the :Af.'. W.·. Brother well says: "ProgreRs in the
sense of' change, can have no favor, yea, no existence with us. Our progress is not in
vain attemptR to change the framework of a syHtem, but, by our own peculiar modes of
applying cardinal principles, to lead up the minds of men in the ways of virtue, and
to school their hearts in all the noble sensibilities." Army Lodges receive no favor
from the Grand Master of Missouri ; but we think the rule adopted by his Grand
Lodge, and one or more others, classing all made in them as clandestine Masons, is
entirely erroneous. We do not believe in these institutions at all, and are glad that
all applications for their organization have been persistently refused by our Grnnd
Master ; but we do not forget that some, perhaps all of those organized, were cst11blished by competent authority, and were probably restricted to proper material; and

views, for as much as that distinguished brother is quite as strenuous as the Nevada.

constitute no part of the landmarks of the institution. If the words the mere
phraseology of the lectures, etc., are a landmark, not admitting of cbang~, and it be
true that our Ancient and Honorable Fraternity originated in the time of King Soloman, or, as some very zealous brethren would have us believe, in the time of Adam
ltimself, then we want to know what business we have with the lectures and other
parts of the work in Anglo Saxon. We must go back to the old Hebrew, or further,
to the language, whatever it was, spoken in the Garden of Eden; or assenting to the
more modern notion of the origin of the work and lectures, we must still rehearse
them in the old style English-and, no matter how many errors in fi:ict, in Biblical
history, and in grammatical constructions we find, we must not touch the phraseology
even in order to remove blemishes, lest some good brother with elongated visage
and upraised hands should cry out against us for making innovations in the body of
Masonry. An<l wlrnt, pray, is the" body of Masonry?" Do the clothes which cover
a man's nakedness constitute any part of his body? We heard a good old lady say
once, wlieu called upon to decide between her own daughter and a step·daughter" the skin is nearer than the shirt." And we think, dechledly, that the words which
clothe and make presentable the grand ideas and glorious truths which do constitute
the body of Masonry, may be and ought to be changed so often as they become old
or obsolete, or better ones, rendering the ideas clearer, and the truths more forcible,
can be found.

The Address of the Grand Master is a well written paper, confined principally to
reporting his official duties. He decfrled, in a case submitted to him, that of an Entered .Apprentice, that a dimit could only be granted to a Master Mason. Taken all
together the decision strikes us as singular, though to the point of granting a dimit
to an Entered Apprentice, we believe, with Bro. CHADWIOK, that it was irregular.
The only proper paper to be given to an Entered ~Apprentice who has removed from
the jurisdiction and desires to receive the remaining degrees in another Lodge, i11 a
certificate to the fact of his making, and a grant of permission to the other Lodge to
finish the work. We are inclined to think, however, that if a dimit had been granted,
it should have been given the el!'cct of the certificate and permit, and the power of
the Lodge granting it been held as cea;;ed-and if, on ap1ilication for the remaining
degrees in the Lodge nearest his rcsi<lcnce, he was rejected, that should be conclusive against his advancement for six monih,; or a year, as the Constitution might provide. We do not see how it could be safely held, that on rejection lie was remanded
to the J,odge making him, and their obligation to Hnish the work renewed. We think
that it would have lJcen much safer to have held that the dimit must have the force
of the proper paper, and that, upon the, application under it to another Lodge, all
authority und all obligation in the first Lodge ceased and detel'mined.• A number of
special dispensations had beeu granted; he had visited as many as possible of his
subordinates, and apologizes to those he did not visit.

1865.-The Eighty-seventh Annual Communication was commenced at tt1e City of
Richmond, on the eleventh day of December. The R.·. W." EDWARD H. LANE was
acting Grand Master, and the W.·. JOHN DovE was Grand Secretary. The M.·. W.·.
WILLIAM H. HARMAN, Grand Master, had departed this life during the recess of the
Grand Lodge.
The Address of Bro. J,ANE is somewhat longer than those of hig predecessors,
though it, too, is brief. The circumsta.ne,es under which the Craft were met are esteemed a cause of thankfulness to the Supreme Architect. Attention is called to the
duties of the hour ; and the legislation necessary to meet some of the consequences
of a state of war continued through four years, is mentioned. He acknowledges the
receipt of a circular conveying information of the formation of the Grand Lodge of
West Virginia, and concedes that it is' not the province of the Grand Lodge to discuss the legality of the State organization. The law is stated, in regard to the establishment of new Grand Lodges, thus concisely and truly : "It is believed to be sound
Masonic law that, the political boundaries of a State being definitely given and de·
cided upon, fixes the Masonic jurisdiction, and this by common consent." He thinks
that it is not best to recognize the new Grand Lodge, or to express any opinion as to
its right to recognition; and inclines to the opinion that unless the individual Lodges
have made returns, and paid dues to, and notified their Grand Lodge of their intention to form a Grand Lodge of their own, any Grand Lodge they might form would
be illegal. A communication from the JW:. W.".JoSEPH D. EvANS, of New York, had
,peen received by Bro. LANE, and was referred to a special committee. The matter
of Union Lodge at Alexandria, and the letter of the Grand Master of the District of
Columbia, are alluded to, and these matters were also referred to a special committee.
We have sufficiently alluded to this in our review of the doings of the District. The
death of Grand Master HARMAN is announced officil1lly, in fitting and affectionate
terms; and on this subject a committee reported appropriate resolutions. The Grand
Lodge determined to clothe the hall in mourniog till the next Annual Communication,
and Bro. WILLIAM F. BUTLER pronounced an eloquent eulogy.
The Finance Committee report that the balance and receipts amounted to
$2,103 49, and the disbursements to $1,116 57-leaving a balance of $986 92.
We esteem it an eminently right and wise step taken by this Grand Lodge, in di·
recting the collection and collation of facts going to show the influence of Masonry
in ameliorating the cruelties of war, and the trials of prison life. These facts, gathered up from the store-house of memory, will serve to enhance the value of Masonic
principles In the eyes of the Fraternity, and do more to rebut the charges made in
the heat of passion, than volumes of argument.
We quote the preamble and resolutions of the committee on the communication
from New York entire, as a matter of interest to all Masons, as men who rejoice at
the removal of every obstacle to the intercourse of brethren in the same grea,t family,
and who have looked forward with longing to the hour when these two influential
• bodies of Freemasons shall be as one.
"WHF.RF.AS, The M.". W:. Grand Lodge of N:ew York has, through its committee,
addressed to the J[:. W.". Grand Lodge of Virginia a very fraternal communication,

tion of the America.n people; that the same antipathies, prejudices and hatreds have
actuated and governed them; but that, nevertheless, during all this sanguinary conflict the gentle and catholic spirit of Masonry has softened animosities, mitigated
hatreds and asserted its beneficent influence over all discordant and contending opinions and elements. It is unnecessary for me to refer to the many instances which. I
might adduce to sustain this assumption, as the facts are too well known to require
particularization or authentication, and are admitted by ail classes of society. But,
brethren, Masonry stops not there; her mission is not yet fulfilled, nor our duties as
Masons yet terminated. There is still a wide' field for our duties and labors. We, as
Masons of the North, should now step forward and extend the right hand of fellowship to our Southern brethren, and endeavor by the influences of kindly feeling and
brotherly love to re-unite the mystic chain which has been so suddenly sundered, and
around our common altars to renew those vows of fraternity which once made and
will again make us the happy children and brotherhood of a common country and
fraternity."

"Bi·o. Elwood Evans, Olympia:

" CHARI,ESTON, S. C., September 18, 1865.

"DEAR SiR AND BROTHER :-1 have received and read with great safofaction your
kind letter of 10th ,June, and should have replied sooner, but waited until I had read
the report of the Committee on Correspondence. * * '" '" '" '" C&ndor compels
me to say, however, that I cannot concur with you in your views of the jurisdictional
question which has been agit 1ting your Grand Lodge and that of Oregon. It is a
settled question of Masonic law, that every Grand Lodge has juri~diction, so far as
relates to grantinl!" of warrants, over all territories not occupied by the eHtablishment
therein of a Grand Lodge ; and that hence in such unoccupied territory there may be
several Lodges which derive their warrants from different Grand Lodges. .This question is, I suppose, admitted as a question of law.
"There remains only the historical question-' was Idaho Lodge, in Idaho city,
in unoccupied territory or not at the time the warrant was granted by the Grand Lodge
of Oregon?' And this depends on another legal .question-' who is to settle ttie
limits of territorial jurisdiction of Lodges, the Grand Lodge themselves or the authority of the country?'
"Now, all past history,all precedent and usage authorizes us to say that Masonic
boundary is coterminous with political boundary. ThPre is no case on record, so far
as I recollect, where the territorial limit of a Grand Lodge was either more or less
than that of a country in which it was situated. The Grand Lodge of England has
the Aame boundary as the kingdom of England-neither more nor less. So the Grand
Lodge of Scotland, of N"ew York, of Ohio, and so on. If the political boundary of a
country is extended, the Masonic boundary of that country is extended in the same
proportion. And if so, then by a parity of reasoning, if the political boundary is diminished, the Masonic is also diminished. Now, by act of Congress (the proper au-
