Bro. LEONIDAS E. PRATT, from the special committee to whom were
referred the Address of the Grand Master and the Annual Report of the
Grand Secretary, presented the following reports:To the M." W. •• Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the Address of the Grand Master, have
examined that paper with diligence and care, and cannot refrain from expre!!!ling
the peculiar pleasure with which its beauty and propriety, its fitness in every respect, its simplicity, precision, and absence of display and ostentation, have filled
us. We consider it, indeed, the legitimate fruit of Masonic teaching, comprehended
and observed ; all its p.arts bearing ample testimony that they have been hewed,
squared, marked, and numbered with the skill of a master workman's hand. W'e
join with our Grand .Master in his congratulations and rejoicings at the peace and
plenty experienced throughout our jurisdiction, since our last Annual Communica·
tion; and lament with him that our brethren in other jurisdictions should have been
less favored than ourselves. We experience, with him, a profound sense of the
, fraternal consideration which we owe to our destitute brethren and their homeless
families, who, on the other side of the continent, have been so long subject to that
"fateful trinity-war, pestilence and famine "-from whose ravflges we have ).lcen
so happily exempt. We join with him, too, in all manner of sympathy and kind·
ness for our brethren beyond the seas, who have lato been subject to the fell spirit
which recently desolated a goodly portion of our own fair land ; and we pray with
a.11 earnestness for the speedy coming of that day when the infiuences of Masonry
shall prevail in every heart, and the nations of the earth learn war no more. We
rejoice, too, as heartily as he can, at the restoration of fratemal relations and intercourse between Grand Lodges which have recently been estranged, and hope, with
like sincerity and fondness, that the same results may be speedily realized in all
remaining cases of that nature. And yet more; we congratulllte this Grand I,odge,
and the Fraternity throughout our jurisdiction, that they have been presided over,
counseled, and directed by the author of the paper we are now conflidcring. With
all due propriety and sense of obligation the Grand .Master expresses his gratitude
to the Craft for the uniform kindness and courtesy with which he has been treated.
We may be permitted to suggest that these are eminently Masonic virtues, and are
to be expected from the Praternity everywhere; but we apprehend that the
brethren hllve never felt that they were thus placing the Grand Master under ob·
ligations to themselves, but rather that they were only, in some small measure,
discharging a debt of gratitude which they owed to him for the zeal and diligence
with which he has so constantly watched, cherished, and protected their interests.
It is the l>rethren, in this case, who are the debtors, and we have no doubt they are
deeply conscious of it.
The reflections and opinions of the Grt1nd Master in regard to amendments to our
Constitution are so just and sensible, and commend themselves so earnestly to the
judgment of every one, that we deem their reference to any committee entirely
uncalled for ; and we recommend at once their approval and indorsement by the
Grand Lodge.
We recommend that the remainder of the Address be apportioned and referred
as follows :To a. special committee of ll.ve, so much thereof as relates to the death of Paet
Grand Master WnLU.li HENRY HOWARD, and Past Deputy Grand .Master PHILIP
WITHAL SHEPHEARD.
To a special committee of seven, so much thereof as relates to .uniformity of
work, and the course to he pursued with those Lodges which have been remiss in
complying with the resolutions of this Grand Lodge in referenee thereto, adopted

To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of Cal.ifornia :Your committee, to whom was referred the Annual Report of the Grand Secretary,
have occuj)ied themselves with the duty thus imposed upon them, and now J>resent
the following as the result of their examination
We may remnrk in the first instance, that tliis is the eleventlt Annual Report of
the present Grand Secretary, and for the eleventh time is this Grand Lodge placed
under many obligations to that most able and faithful officer. The fact of this long
retoution in tlmt position, alone, is perhaps the highest compliment that Bro. ABELL
could receive. A body constituted as this is, cannot be hoodwinked or deceived; and,
exacting, as Masonry does, both capt1city and diligence in 1111 stations, long service
is conclusive evidence of accompanying worth and merit. Bnt a careful scrntiny
and analysis of the report now before us leads irresistibly to the same conclusion.
The real facts, llnd the appearances on the surface, are in perfect harmony ; and they
unite to establish the certainty that our good brother has earned and deserved all
the honors he has received. We might, perhaps, be accused of vanity should we proclaim that we have the best Grand Sem·etary on this continent; hut we do challenge
all·the Grand Secretaries in the world, to excel in the aggregate the good works of
our own. What we particultl.rl,y admire and commend in the paper before us, is its
perfect method and conciseness. It emboilies in detail and with minuteness all the
many transactions of tlrnt otllce, yet it will occupy but few pages in your printed
volume. In this re~pect it i~ a triumph of skill. Few reports of this character and
magnitude, embracing so great a variety of matter, are so framed and finished as to
be comprehended and understood throughout at the first reading. This is one of the
exceptional cases. The report is made as the business of the office has been inva·
riably conducted. Neither can be too highly commended.
The Fraternity is also under renewed obligations to Bro. ABELL for his continued
zeal and interest in the .Masonic Library. The report shows several valuable ad·
ditlons to thnt collection; and as the uses and advantages of such an institution cannot be over-estimated, so should we manifest a proportionate· appreciation of the
services which tend to its improvement and perfection. Two valuable old vol11mes
have been presented by Bro. WILLIAM L. MAULE, of Virginia. This is not the first
time that the thanks of this Grand Lodge have !;teen due to Bro. MAULE fur his con·
tri\Jutions; and, if we cannot reciprocate the favors, we can at least be as grateful
as our distinguished brother is kind and generous. He is doubtless acting by the
well known admonition, that" it is more blessed to give than to receive."

The W.·. LEONIDAS E. PRATT, Grand Orator, then delivered the Annual
Oration, as follows:MOST WORSRlPFt:L GRAND MASTER
AND BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LoDGE : -

Once more the revolving years and happy chances of our lives bring us· together
in counsel, homage, and devotion; and the favor of our esteemed Grand Master has
devolved on me the performance of a task, for which riper years and larger ex·
perieuce in the Craft far better might have qnalifled me. Were this an occasion on
which the doctrine of compensations might be legitimately invoked·-could I hope
that the zeal and· devotion of the young enthusiast would be ac1;epted as the equiv~
alent of that wisdom and learning, that eloquence and beauty which ought to adorn
the effort of the ·honr, then might I anticipate a share of your approbation; but only
by snch substitution; only by some magical transformation of that which falls from
the lips to that which is hidden in the heart-of the cold words uttered to the warm
sentiment experienced-can I expect to realize your commendation. But enough,
rny brethren, of preface and apology; for it is the distinguishing characteristic of
the institution in whose name and interests we are to·day assembled, that it requires
on all occasions the existence of merit, and accepts no excuse or apology for its
absence. Let us, then, address ourselves to the pleasant and welcome, but no less
difficult, task before us.
From time immemorial, and in almost every land, there has existed an association, strange and mysterious to the outer world, but simp!e, beautiful, and lovely to
those who have passed its portals and reveled in the moral and intellectual treasures
hidden within. We wonder not that such associations were organized in the earliest
ages, for the Creator had so finished His work as to involve their necessity. Man, by
the wisdom of infinite intelligence, was kindly made dependent ou his fellowmanendowed with a nature which required, and a disposition which imperatively de·
manded, tho joys and amenities of social life. We wonder not that solemn cov·
enants were made, for God himself had given our fathers the example. We wonder
not that in the primal ages, fraternal relations should have been diligently culti·
vated; for the moral and intellectual elements predominated in man, and these fac·
nlties, Jilte the physical powers, must have food and exercise. Neither do we wonder

1

1866.]

Grand Lodge of California.

397

that these associations were select and exclusive; that barriers were set up whic'b.
turned back the multitude, and over wbich the few alone could pass; for In the
mornin/:( of man's existence, as to·day, not all were.worthy of esteem and fellow·.
ship. But when we realize only in part the ·wonders of man's progress from that.
age to 'this; when we consider how vast the changes which have transpired, and how
varied and wonderful the growth and development of his moral and intellectual
nature; when we reflect how empires have risen, flourished, and been overthrown,
and nations have been swept from tl1e face of tlie eart11-how all things else have
been marked by the finger of decay and desolation-how sects and systems have
been broken up and dissipated, and one dl~pensation followed another in quick sue·
cession to the tomb; when we look around upon the world of to·day,aud study its insti·
tutions and the existing relations of our race to flnd in them scarcely a fact, feature,
or principle wbh'h we seem to hold in common witn the patriarchal age; when we
consider how often and with what terrible elfect society has been revolutionized.and
its foundations broken up and destroyed; we may well wonder that an a~sociation
then formed should have endured these changes and mutations, and come down to
us with its 'material features as they were when the morning star~Fang togeth~r, with
even its forms and ceremonies unaltered in any essential particular since the time
when the first civilization and the lost arts reared tl1ose stupendous monuments
whicll are the wonders even of this wonderful age-when the wisest of men dis·
tributed to the patient builders the well earned rewards of persistent toil and
fidelity to duty. But if we wonder that the i;ssociation itself should have been thus
preserved, simply, bow much more must we marvel that in every age, through all the
transitions of society and in every stnge of its development, in darkness or in light,
in progression or retrogression, in ci.vilizatlon or in barbarism, in peace or war, in
freedom or in bondage, It has supplied the wants, administered to the joys, and
solaced tlie sorrows of all who have claimed its patronage, with the same measure of
skill and success. Not only in every age, hut in every land and to every race and every
rank: in life it has been equally available and u8eful; nnd more than that, grandly ennobling and instructive. The cllild of the forest, unsltilled either in science or
theology, but !istenhg with reverential awe for th~ whisperings of the Great Spirit;
the Hindoo, cultivated in the subtle but sophistical lore of priest and Brahmin, prostrate at the shrine of the Pagoda; the. Parsee, in his false but fascinating worship;
the follower of Mahomet, bowing to the east in morning prayer; the son of Judea
on the sacred Mount; the Greek Christian, the Latin. the Catholic and the Protestant
alike; the descendants of the Northman and the Druids, standing in solemn awe by
the hallowed sites of their rude and ancient temples; the listener by the ruins of tile
Parthenon and (Jo!iseum; the child of the desert, sweeping its burning sands as swift
and !i8tless as tllo winds th11t fan his brow; the wanderer amid the mouldering obelisks
and pillars of Greece, and ltome, and Babylon, and Tyre; all, all, savo the fool whu
l1ath said in his heart there is no God, have shared its glories and learned its mystio
language, observed its covenants, and bowed iu cheerful submission to its divine
commands. Prince and pcasl\nt, priest and luyman, the ruler and the ruled, have
gazed with the same awe upon its hieroglyphic light, and worn witll the same pride
and pleasure its pure habiliments and mystic emblems. They have knelt together by
the same altar. and, ri8ing with the new light from the refulgent East beaming in
upon their souls, have joined hands in the same solemn vows, and kept those vows with
the same zeal and fldelity through all the trials and exigencies of their varied liyes
and experiences. Universal as the universe, and wide-spread as humanity itself, its
temples are the symbols of the world we fnhahit; long as from east to west, wide e.s
between north and south, and covered, as such vastness only can be covered, by the
clonde<l canopy which stretches away to tlie confines of boundless space. So are'
the duties it enjoins upon its disciples equally extensive, embracing all the conceivable relations of humanity. The spiritual edifice is symbolized by the material in alt

398

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 11,

its parts, and the extent of one is the chief beauty and glory of the other. What'
then, my brethren. shall be said of the wisdom which could contrive, so far back in
the world's history that the earth itself seems to glide from under us, and even tradition slips away from our grasp, an institution which, unchanging in itself, should
still be found adapted to the wants of all ages, of every people, to conditions of
society which were the very antipodes of each other? Six thousand year~. with all
their ceaseless changes and requirements, lrnve proved mankind .incapable of an7
conditions or organizations to which this association is not perfectly adapted without
the slightest innovation upon its original form or character. Is there a problem
more difficult to solve? Can anything more incomprehensible than this be presented
to the eye of philosophy? Has aught else, the creation of human intellect and
genius, survived? If this be the work of man exclusively, tho fruits of his unaided
efforts, how has it escaped the tide of destruction which has overwhelmed and
swallowed up all else? What power has bid Time st1>y his ruthless baud-what
guardian ~pirit has held the shield between it and decay and dissolution?
The material structures, reared with all the skill and ingenuity of the wisest in.the
past, and then designed and hoped to be perpetual-the splendid edifice-the massive
pile-the brass and marble monuments which commemorated the good or evil d?eds
of those who reared them-all have perished; and the very dust of their decay, like
that of their architects, their founders and projectors, can be no more distinguished
from the common mass of common clay. Where, indeed, are the institutions which
were coeval with its birth? On the ".ery spot where its infancy was cradled a scqre
of nations have since risen, flourished, and expired; and no morrow's sun shall ever
dawn on them, to chase the gloom aud darkness of their starless night. By the tomb
of Achilles and the palaces of Priam the slavish herdsman tends his flocks; and the
wandering Arab, unconscious of the faded glory which has come down to us through
the page of history and the glimmer of tradition, pitches his rude tent by tl!e shattered columns of some proud old city of the dead past, and pillows his head on the
crumbling fragments of thrones and crowns! "Passing away," bus been written on all
by tho inexorable hand of hard and cruel fate, and the earth we tread seems now but
one vast sepulchre, in which lie buried both the works and hopes of all who have
gone before us.
In the moral world decay and desolation !1ave been still more triumphant and
complete. Governments of every shad<!', from the Theocracy-from the fearful absolutism of the Turk and Russ-to the pure Democrncy of ancient Poland; social, political, and religious associations of every hue and character; systems, sects, philosophies, dispensations, creeds, and religiOl)S themselves; have come forth like vernal
leaves, and like them perished in the breath of autumn. In the material universe
there is but one parallel in time and duration-the Pyr8.rnids of Egypt, which stand
alone mocking the consuming rust of centuries; in the moral world there is no vestige
of the like endurance. And, as the Pyramids have stood for ages, and muRt endure
for ages yet to come, ever baffling the efforts of science and the mechanic arts to discover the secret of their construction and exemption from decay, so in the moral
world this institutio.n, whose most excellent temits have been transmitted unimpaired through all the ages, shall endure forever; numbering among its patrons more
men of lawful age than all the religious sects of the world combined; more potent
than kingdoms and principalities, and ever baffling every effort to find in the wisdom
of man the capacity to project and complete its organization. I repeat, the wisdom
which contrived this association is far bvond the depth and range of our poor humanity. Where, then, shall we look for its origin, except to Heaven and the giver
of all good? As the design of its first.material temple was first given by God to its
founder, so the wisdom which designed that moral and spiritual edifice, which has
survived the destruction of its sanctuary at Jerusalem to bless mankind to-day, could
be no less than the wisdom of the Supreme Architect Himself. It has endured be-

1866.J

Grand Lodge of California.

899

cause it is the work of Him whose creations cannot be destroyed. It is unchanging,
universal, and eternal, because these are the attributes of its author, and the char·
acter and qualities of its divine progenitor have been by Him impressed upon His
handiwork.
Its fortunes, too, have been as varied as the times in which it has existed. In every
age it has been tossed and buffeted over tempestuous seas, lashed into fury by the
storms of persec.ution. On every field of fame its sous have bared their bosoms to
the charge and turned the tide of battle for the right.. Their arms have been upraised
wherever truth has been assail~d or human rights imperiled. They have followed
honor and sealed their devotion to her with their lives, wherever she has led, over
seas, across !ontinents and empires, even to the home of the Savionr and the site of
the sacred sepulchre. In the dark ages, when its sublime truths were unappreciated,
and its glorious purposes unknown and belied, its enemies arose on llvery hand, numberW,ss as leaves in the forest, or sands by the sea-shore. Kings and Princes betrayed
and persecuted it. The power of empires was wielded with the vengeance and bitterness of offended royalty, to crush and destroy it. Fire and the sword-all the agencies
of destruction which malignity could invent, were arrayed against it. Its temples
were despoiled and its treasures dissipated. Its children have been robbed, and
hunted like wild beasts from the face of the earth. They have been politically proscribed and socially discarded; the channels of commerce have been closed against
them; and business even has shunned them as unfit to be the second parties to a
sil)lple contract. Reviled and persecuted-the tortures of the rack and inquisition
have been invoked, and bigotry, in the name and guise of religion, has pursued them
with the remorseless zeal of fanaticism and hate. All the influences of common enmity
and rancor'"the hope of reward and the fear of punishment and destruction-the
threats of power and its blandishments alike have all been unavailing. They have
still ref.used to lay down their faith or abandon their vows, and thus the grand old institution of the patriarchal age has still survived. ·Few and feeble, they J1ave been
driven from its altars to the mountains, the wilderness, and the cave; but returning
with deeper faith and devotion, they have rekindled brighter than before its sacred
fires. What else, the work of man, has endured so much unbroken, and preserved its
power and vitality unimpaired? What, tlien, my brethren, shall be said of the strength
which has supported it through all the years of its trials, and against all the assaults
of numberless enemies? Has the power of nian alone been adequate to support that
which he had not the wisdom to contrive? Can it be less than the Omnipotence of
the Infinite which has preserved and sustained it? And may we not justly claim a
divine origin for that which divinity seems to have specially cherished and protected?
Turn, now, from the wisdom which contrived, and the strength which has supported, to the contemplation of that marvel om beauty which adorns the mystic edifice, and behold again how apt and beautiful the analogy; how perfect the harmony
and correspondence betwe•,n the spiritual and the material structures. Study, if you
please, the ravishing beauty of the first Temple, fitly reared on the sa;red spot where
the fidelity of the stricken Patriarch had heen so severely tested, to commemorate
that virtue which he so eminently displayed, and commend its practice to succeeding generations. Contemplate the grandeur and magnificence of that stat.ely edifice;
its lavish display of wealth; its gorgeous finish; the splendor of its onrament and
decoration ;-tlie grandest triumph of human art, it stood unrivaled, unapproached,
and unapproachable; its peerless beauty, the endearing theme of song and inspiration, fitly hallowed by the manifest presence of the Deity Himself-worthy to be his
dwelling-place on earth! So the spiritual temple, then organized and then perfected,
springing from and engrafted upon its material protot.ype and the operative art which
reared it, stands in the moral world without precedent, parallel, or approximation;
its moral beauty and adornment unapproached by any association which the skill

[Oct. 11,_

and ingenuity of man has devised in twice three thousand years. The relation of
the first Temple to the now existing association, of the material to the moral ~trnc·
ture, is the relation of the mortal body to the immortal soul. As the body is the
most wonderful of all the material works of the Creator, so was the Temple the
grandest result of human power and ingenuity; iis the former gro"'.s in sil~nce and
comes we know not whence, so in silence grew the Temple-the mystic creat10n of the
will of its Grand Architect. Our bodies perish and depay: so has the Temple fallen
by the ravages of time. But as the human soul, the ge~ enshri?ed within, i.s t~e far
better and nobler part of us, so does the spiritual edifice which dwelt w1thm the
Temple o:i th 3 sacred mnunt, far exceed In worth and glory the m:1g11i~cent cradle
in which. it was nursed Into vigor and power ; and as the soul shall live forever to

There, too, on the self same spot, the doom had been lil'ted from the child of
Abraham-death had been stayed and the destroyer vanquished. Bo the mysteries
of the Temple, and its moral counterpart so cherished now, teach as ~hey should,
and teach with more emphasis and power than all the eloquence of pulpit and press
combined, the lessons of a resurrection and a second life. It Is in fact a religions
associatiou, and we may marvel much that this character should have ever been de·
nied it; not religious in any narrow or restricted sense; not Chris.tian.' nor Jewish, nor
Pagan, nor Mahometan, nor Catholic, nor Protestant, but only, sunpty and purely re·
ligious. Religion, be it remembered, is of God. Sects, forms, ~n.d nam:s a'.e the works
of men. It is uni'VerBalrellgion which it inculcates; that rehg1on which 1t deems es·

responsibility which affords the only security for the faithful observance of its ~wn
pure principles and solemn vows. A belief in the existence .of a Supreme Bemg i
the certainty and justice of His judgments; and the ilnmortahty of the soul ;-these
are the elements of religion which it requires in its votaries, while it heeds not the
forms and specific articles of fnith, which sects have set up and dignified w.itb Ure
appellation of the only true rellgiou. It has indeed been the sanctua? of tins unlveral religion from ita first inception. To preserve the knowledge of the true God
from the assaults of Paganism in the dark days when idolatry possessed all the world
save the little land of Judea and its chosen people, was the sole purpose and object
of its first organization. It was only through the esoteric workings of some such
association, that that knowledge could be preserved; and when asked why those
sublime truths, so good and commendable, should be veiled within the Temple, we
only need remember that for teaching them publicly, even in enlightened Athens, a
gtellt and good philosopher was doomed to die. It has preserved that knowledge
through those periods. when but for it, that knowledge must snrely have been lost.
It has faithfully and efficiently performed that high and holy mission. It hus <Jome
down to our da¥ and generation with the religious feature In Its character unim·
paired, and it
cease to be the institution which has been transmitted to us, when
it ceases to inculcate religion; not indeed the peculiar religion of Paul or Moses, or
Calvin or Luther, but that which, commanding and requiring us to recognize and
adore a Great J<'irst Co.use, to look for judgment on our deeds, and Invoke the aid of
Deity in all our laudable undertakings; which, compelling us to clothe and feed and
cherish as our own the friendless and the destitute, to visit the widow o.nd t11e father·
'less, and keep ourselves unspotted from the world; yet leaves us wi~in the range of
these grand duties and landmarks, to adopt our own forms of worship and peculiar
dogmas, to ap1iroach the throne of Almighty pbwer as our preferences may suggest,
and adore Him under whatever na.me we choose, be it God, Jehovah, Jove, or Lord.
Such is the grand, the beautiful, the broad, the liberal, and comprehensive religion
which it inculcates. It embraces all its substance without its forlll!l. It includes the

In that !Ill.me general sense it is also a political association; not political in the.
modern and corrupted sense, but only in that pure significance which confines the.
application of the term to government, while it ignores, abhors p1trty and pnrty
inlluences and interests. Devotion to government it fosters and cultivates with untiring zeal; but the presence of party influence would be deemed the most ignoble
desecration of its sacred temple. It teaches simply the great duties which man owes
at all times to tile government under which he lives, whatever be its form or policy;
to be a peaceful citizen, faithful and obedient to the law ; and within the outline
thus prescribed it declines to know even, much less to dictate, his particular faith or
associations. The leading features of good government-order and obedience-it in.
ct1lcates mnre e!factua.lly than any existing organization ; for that which too often is
but theory elsewhere, .is const'lnt practice here-the maintenance of perfect discipline being essential to the administration of its own internal a!fairs. Within
itself it is indeed at once a pure democracy and an absolute despotism. It is demo'.
era.tic in placing all upon a common level, and trying all by the same emblem o!
virtue and morality; in abrogating all distinctions of caste, quality and birth; and
making that merit which dwells within and manifests itself by noble deeds and
kindly elforts the only passport to preferment. Not one of all the multitt1de within
its fold who is not eligible to the highest honors in the Craft ; not one so poor that
he would be deemed pretentious ln thus aspiring. The ballot place!! in every hand,
the humblest is as potent as his royal brother can be. Yet, with this the very
essence of despotism is blended. It is despotic in the eiiforoement of its laws and
regulations. lt is despotic in making the will of the Master the absolute law of the·
Craft, and in exacting prompt and implicit obedience to his decisions and commands,
whatever they may be, though it imposes no restraint upon his discretion save the
moral power of his fraternal relations and the obligations he has taken. Nor are
any di8tinctions there found in the application of discipline an.d penalties. Nobles,
Monarchs, aud Princes, have alike been subject to them. The profane or vulgar
utterance of the poorest and lowliest in all the Brotherhood would be as promptly
punished if it fell from the lips of the King who swayed the scepter over millions.
No hesitations, no questions, no murmurings are tolerated, and no remoniltrances can
be heard. Obedience thus taught and thus enforced becomes, in time, a portion of
their very natures, and they cease to know there can be such a thing as resistance to
legal authority. The members of a society thus organized and conducted must be
better citizens by reason of such associations. They cannot fail to re1·erence and
appreciate the principles of government, and when all mankind have been im·
b.ued with the same spirit and subject to a like discipliee, the horrors of civll strife
and insurrections will come to us no more forever. What wonder that in every age
it has received the patronage, the aid, and encouragement of Kings and Cabinets;
a.nd the rulers of every land have sought to ally themselves with its potential in·
fiuences. Look into your own army and navy, the Legislative, Executive, Judii:ial,
and Ministerial Departments"of your own most excellent government, and yon wlll
find three·fifths of all tlie leading and official characters chosen from the long·
honored association; while the whole number bears to the whole mass of citizens
eligible to such positions, the proportion perhaps ofless than one to five. Then look
abroad. Take.in, at one grand review, the whole civilized world. Search the rec·

porti~n. There can be but one reason assigned for .this. It is because the internal
govemment and discipline of the association itself has better fitted and prepared its

Again, my brethren, it is most preeminently a social institution. Literally, ln·
deed, there could be no union, no association in the absence of the social qualities
in it~ constituent parts. But we mean here something more than this narrow sense
implies, We mean that both the design and the tendency and elfect of the nssocJ.
ation, is to enlarge and promote that true sociality, that kindne~s of heart, that
com·tesy and hospitality, whicb so much improve and adorn the character, and the
absence of which is the chief vice of savage life. The influences exerted in this
direction cannot be over.estimated. There, around the same altar where all have
bowed the knee and assumed identical obligations, again, and again, and again, until
the sands of life are exhausted, meet the brethren of every business and profession,
of every sect and opinion, gathered in from all the walks of life. The high and low,
rich and poor, learned and unlearned, King and subject, walk together, arm in arm,
on the same level, untrammeled by thE> artificial and too -often invidious <listinctiollil
of what the world is pleased to call society. It is the free and generous intercourse
of those who are in perfect accord, whose tongues and hearts ever unite in promoting
each other's welfare and n·joicing at each other's prosperity. It is the attrition of
sou.I ag,iiost soul-mind against mind-receiving, imparting, blending, an<l commingling. There the unlearned gathers knowledge from the lips of his more favored
brother ; and even the collegiate professor and master of JJhilosopbies may sometime
draw wisdom from the native sense and vigorous intellect of his uncultivated associ·
ate. In the interchange of views and opinions all may participate without restraint.
There is no fear of scoff or ridicule, of jeers or sarcasm, for all are brethren, ani·
mated by thp, same spirit of kindness and fellowship; while, beyond their faithful
breusts, uot a word there uttered can ever pasR. There are no leaders, favorites, or
orators. The same deference is extended, the same freedom tolerated, and the same
rules of intercourse are applied to all. The heart, too, as well as mind, is busy. The
sorrows and distresses of the absent are presented, sympathy is kindled, and t11c finest
feelings are awakened to activity. Tbey vie with each other only in relieviug the distressed ; they emulate each other in contributions to ·the rational enjoyment of all.
Thus the nobler parts of man, the mind and heart, are cultivated, strengthened, and
expanded by constant exercise. The soul is filled with kinder sentiments, wi1J1 higher
hopes and nobler aspirations, and man is advanced in the scale of being towards the
status of that Supreme Intelligence, after whose image he was formed.

And yet again, my brethren, it is a scientific association. Who has passetl the
Middle Chamber without feeling more keenly than ever before the weakness of uncultivated intellect-without resolving henceforth to apply his powers with renewed
vigor to the mastery of the arts and sciences? What a rich and boundless field for
study and refiection is there opened up! 'With what new charms are the wondei·ful
Arcana of nature clothed and exhibited! Long years before, with patient toll, t}er·
haps he may have mastered and admired the elements of geometry; but where else
had he been taught to apply its principles to the culture of morality? Where else bad
this wonderful use-this additional charm-been given to that practical science? So,
too, in other schools he may have studied and admired the science of architecture.
But where else had its implements been presented as the emblems of virtue, and the
marvelous beauty of their hidden significance revealed? Where else has he been
taught that, as a proper application of the rules of those sciences in the inaterial
world would result in the production of those structures which have been the wonder
and admiration of all time, so in the moral world the observance of their ~nalogies
would clothe our characters with that moral beauty which shall open up to us the
joys of that 'silent land which lies, in eternal peace and sunshine, over the River of
Death. Ah! beautiful! beautiful ! indeed, as a moral science, stands the proud old
souvenir of the primeval world, and sterile is the heart on which it• sunshine falls
without effect. Cold and senseless as mortal clay must be the immortal spirit which
sees no added charm in art and science, when tl1ey are thus made the ministers of
our future joys, the lights which guide us to the haven of eternal rest.
And still, again, my brethren, proud and prominent among the many noble
features of thls association stands that priceless virtue which shall cover many sins-Charity, That charity which leads to alms-giving and the practice of benevolence
in onr daily lives; that spirit which bids us stoop and bind the strangers' wounds
when Pl'iest and Levite have come, and gazed, and passed by on the other sidethese, the noblest elements of human character, it fosters with especial zeal and
care. And here, again, it is the pride and glory of the Order that it teaches these
lessons, as it does general morality, with n power and eftlciency which aU the
teachers of the universe, from Christ and his dh;ciples down, have ever failed to ex·
ercise. Enter the temple, traverse its ground floor only with attentive mind, and
there learn that the proph,ets and poets of the olden time were but feeble masters of
the parable and symbol-cl1ildren only iu the art of teaching. Wllat could be more
effective and impressive than the earne;t demand, so startling to the neophyte in his
poverty and destitution; that be comply with the immemorial custom of the Frater·
nity 1 Could the lessons of charity tte more forcibly presented? That beautiful illus·
tration of the grandest of virt11es can never be forgotten. Years may pass and the
,ceaseless changes of time bury all else In oblivion, but the remembrance of that will
still remain. The good or evil fortuues of life may gladden or depress; joy or sor·
row, hope or despair, prosperity or adversity, may be his companions; but the pleas·
ing memories of that hour still liuger in the mind and rise up on every hand to
soften the heart whenever want and aftliction are presented for solace and relief.
Who could pass that ordeal without a keener sense of his own dependence on his
fellow man and a higher appreciation of his own binding obligations as a member of
the great social compact? Its remembrance comes back to him through all the
a,fter years, by day and by night, in the busy haunts of men, in the seclusion of the
chamber or the studio-ever reminding him of the nakedll'\ss and de~titntion with
which he came into the world, of the vanity of wealth and po~r, and of the fraternal
assistance which he owes his fellow man. It sends him ont into'the dark spots of the
world on the divine mission of benevolence and love. It bids him alleviate human
suffering wherever it is found, biu~ up the broken heart, and point the erring to that
blissful realm beyond the grave, where tears are wiped from all eyes, and pain
and sorrow cannot enter, By the sick bed and at the grave, in the homes of the

marvellous salvation? What but its divinity should preserve it when all else perished,
and for what important mission in the unknown future has it been thus favored? We
know, indeed, that in the fnture, as in the past, it shall go on doing good to all-t~ach·
ing virtue antl enforcing its practice-showering its golden blessings like the gentle
dews of Heaven, unseen and unfelt, save in the general joy and freshness everywhere
imparted. Let us hope, my brethren, that in that future it may have no other mission
to perform ; yet the thought will sometimes arise that pos>ibly that other experience
of the past may yet be repeated. We have already seen that within this association
alone, for many years, was the knowledge of the true God preserved from the ravages of
Paganism; that but for it Idolatry would have been universal, and, in the absence of
new revelations from Heaven, perpetual also. How vast, indeed, the debt of gratitude
which civilization owes it now! for whatever is great and good in the science of gov·
ern.nent, whatever is commendable in the practices of private life, whatever has
elevated and improved the character of man, whatever is promotive of knowledge
and virtue here and calculated to secure peace and joy in the great hereafter, bas
gone hand in hand with true religion around the earth, following wherever she has
led, and halting wherever she has paused. By preserving the one, it bas secured to
us the .other. May it be suggested now, with painful apprehensions, that somewhere
iu the future the pall of barbarism may again enshroad the world-the corruption of
life again eventuate in Idolatry-and the kindly offices of this organization be once
more required to preserve through another period of darkness the mysteries it so
fondly and persistently cherished heretofore. May it be asked, then, if this was indeed
the design and purpose of its Divine Author in the beginning-the reason of its won·
derful preservation by His interposition, through all the perils which environed and
assttiled it?
What, my brethren, is this association, so divine in its character, so marvelous in
its organization, so unchanging and endurable in all its features, so useftil in the daily
walks of life, so fruitl'ul of eternal good to those who obey its lessons, so beautiful
and lovely without, so instructive iind enchanting within? Who has failed to recog·
nize the association thus presented? You, indeed, who have sllared its honors and
enjoyed its ble>s:ngo, who lrnve stood within its sacred portals, enraptured by
its beauty and glorified in its spiritual presence, might be expected to respond with
one accord. But, my brethren, you needed not that discivline or experience ; you
needed not to have entered the holy of holies, traversed the middle chamber, nor
even to have knelt on the ground floor of its gorgeous temple, to enable you to
answer. 1'he mass of men, the ignorant, the rejected, the profane, they who have
never gaze 1 upon the light which Craftsmen only may behold, know that in al! the
vast world around us, with all its wonders and achievements, there is but one institution which can till the~e outlines, and it is called FREEMASONRY. I say, with studied
care, that the8c clements, these virtues and feahires, when thus combined, are called
Freemasonry; but they do not constitute that art. The promotion of every virtue,
the improvement 'of character, the practice of morality and the re lief of distress-these are the fruits, the clfects of Masonry. The secret work, its rituals, lectures,
forms, ceremonies, signs. und ~ymbols-th.;se are but the habiliments in whkh it is
clothed. They are the visible body. Masonry itself is the invisible soul within,
which pervades and animates, adorns and deifies that body. Alas! that so many,
even of our own household, should mistake what we technically call the work of
Masonry, for Masonry-the outward clothing for the vital, active principle within.
Its outward apparel, its material .temples, and all its tangible features are indeed
lovely and beautiful beyond conception. They speak to the outward senses with a
charm and precision which no other language can possess; yet they are but the
drnpery which aaorns the goddess-the simple medii through which her sons are
known and recognized in the outer world. We marvel at, we study and admire
them. While their meaning is yet concealed, we are delighted even at what often

seems but empty form, because of the method and propriety, the grace and ,dignity,
the order and solemnity which accompany every step of the mysterious process.
But when the strange and novel ceremonies are ended, and the senses are no longer
occupied with crowding forms and symbols, we return to the East, and heart and
mind alone are there addre~serl. Then, from the chair of the ancient King, the wisest
man and first Grand Master, the instructive tongue 110urs out its rich, exhaustless
treasure. The reason of each ceremony is then revealed. Step by step, with the
care and precision of natural science, the hidden significance of every act is disclosed, every form and symbol is interpreted. We are lost in wonder at the artistic
skill whfoh clothes the virtues in such gorgeons drapery, which makes the frigid and
repulsive lessons ot' the worldly schools a beauteous and enchanting science. Then,
indeed, the conception of poetry is reallze!l-then vice is in truth presented, as
"A monster of such frightful mien,
That to be hat~d, needs but to be seen."
There the virtues which we have been constrained, unwillingly, perhaps, to practice, are clothed anti garnished with a beauty and adornment which makes their
faithful ob~ervance a luxury and charm. With pleasure we pursue the study until
the work of Masonry is all acquired; and, perfect in every detail and particular, we
are prepared to serve with honor and precision in any position, from the Grand East
to the outer door. We turn our attention then to its jurisprudence-that grand old
monument of the wisdom of the early fathers; more ancient, mnre replete with the
learning and philosophy of law than the works of all the jurists and lawgivers of the
profane worlrl combined. It is the very eclecticism of all other systems; it is the
perfection of human reason, pervaded by the unerring justice of heaven. We explore
and ma~ter all its det11.ils; we make ourselves living digests of Masonic law. We
are ready on the instant to solve with certainty all questions of discipline and administration. Ko difficulty can arise so complex in its character that we do not
point at once the appropriate remedy and guide tlie inquirer in the way to justice.
We study, next, its history and traditions; devour its written volumes and treasure
up in the storehouse of memory all that can be known o'f the venerable institution.
We attend with scrupulous punctuality the stated convocations of the Craft ; we pay
our monthly dues with caret'nl promptitude; and we contribute to tlie wants of those
around us whenever their miseries are presented at our doors. All this accomplished, in the technical language of the Fraternity, we are pronounced" bright
Masons."
Let us not, my brethren, thus deceive ourselves. How mean, how vile, how
hollow and contemptible is the Masonic charncter, which extends no farther, and
embraces no more than the cold, constrained and formal discharge of thcHe ohlill"a·
tions. lfasonry itself is something more than ceremonies, forms, and symbol~. It is
a spirit-the spirit of God manifesting itself in purity and 110wer, through the beautiful language and material emblems, devised by man with Hi• Almighty a.it.I and coun·
sel. We may know its history and traditions, its achievements and jurisprudence;
we may wander through its mystel"ious chambers, understanding and interpreting its
symbolism ; we may be learnerl in its lectures and masters of its secret work, and
yet the volume of Masonry be to us a sealed an<l ~ilent book. W c may know its requirements and disregard them-under:<tand the duties it enjoins, and not o hserve
them. We may admire its spirit, aud refuse that spirit a dwelling place within our
souls; its lessons may have fallen on our hearts like grateful rains upon the vast Sa·
hara-producing no fruits, but leaving behintl only the desolate waste of former years.
We may have appreciated and admired the !Jeauty, symmetry, and perfection of its
ceremonies, its leetnres, and its law, hut if we have failed to observe that
these are but the avennes which lend us up to the moral edifice beyond, that they ar\l
only emblems of the like qualitie,; in the spiritual strnctnre-Masonry itself-then, indeed, our lessons and our toils have been in vain. But the kindly spirii, the senti-

BURNS, from the action of Progress Lodge, No. 125, expelling him from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry, report as follows:The charge against the accused was substantially that of fraudulently alleging, in a petition presented by him to said Lodge for the degrees of Masonry,
"that he had resided in the State of California more than. one year, and in the city
of San Francisco more than six month", next preceding his application, and that he
had not, within twelve months, been rejected by any Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons ;" wherea<, in truth and in fact, he had resided in the city of Virginia, State
of Nevada, for some time previous to, and within two months of, the presentation of
said petition, and had been rejected for the degrees by Escurial Lodge, No. 7, in
the State of Nevada, within three months of the date of his application to Progress
Lodge.
Your committee have given the testimony in the case (which is rather volumin·
ous) a careful ex 1mination, and have heard all that could be urged on behalf of the
accused; and, after mature deliberation, they are of the opinion that the record clearly
shows that the accused had actually been a resident of Nevada, and not of Califor.
nia, within the year referred to. The proof on that point consists of his own sworn
statement, made in April, 1865, in the State of Nevada, for the purpose of registra·
tion as a voter, in which he claimed that State as the place of his" actual," and not
"constructive,'' residence. This is only opposed by the testimor.y of certain wit·
nesses that his family resided here, and that they believed, from his declarations,
that this was his residence; and by the suggestions of the accused that, after his return
to California, in November, 18G5, he di,;covered, on consultation with his counsel, that
he had made a mistake in claiming Nevada as his residence-that California was-and
that he might vote in California in November, 18G5, which he did. Although resi·
dence is, for the most part, a question of intention, and can be changed at the volition
or the party, yet we think it cannot be claimed reasonably that mere declarations
would he received as authoritative to contradict a sworn statement to the contrarythat statement being sworn to for the purpose of obtaining and exercising a right
growing out of such statement. We think, therefore, that the averments in the
petition, upon the question of residence, were untrue.
In a like position, beyond cont.roversy, stands the statement that he had not been
rejected by any Lodge during the year, for we have before ns his original petition,
presentEN. in August, 1865, to the Lodge in the State of Nevada. The accused, how·
ever, sceRs to avoid these conclusions by endeavoring to prove that he signed the
petition without reading lt carefully, or without being aware of its contents. Apart
from the question of the manifest impropriety-in fact, culpable neg'igence of such
a proceeding on the part of an applicant for our degrees, we think the record does
not sustain him in this position. He hims~lf says, in his testimony," that he did not
ren,d the petition through, hut merely glanced over it-thought it was ril!;ht-would
not have signed it if he had known the full contents thereof." Yet, in his answer to
the charges, he does not aver his ignorance of the misstatements in his petition, but
seeks to evade them by raising a technical question. He says that, after discovering
that his legal residence was in San Francisco, and that therefore the reception of his
petition in the State of Nevada was" improper and illegal," and having been informed that a rejection under such an" illegal reception" was a nullity, and that
therefore the rejection left him prec!sely where he was before he applied there, he
signed the petition here ; and denies any fraud or the suppression of any " material
truth" in the case.
Viewing this testimony and answer together, we feel satiSfied that the Lodge was
justified in holding that the applicant must have known that the material facts of
reside11ce and rejection were not truly stated in !iis petition, and that he perhaps
thought the technical position he had assumed shielded him from th~ averment of a
falsehood. We thus find the main facts in the case, by preponderance of testimony,

against the accused. 'l'hat, then being assumed, the question occ11rs, wos the judgment of the Louge in the premi~es correct? We are of the opinion that it was.
When an applicant presents his petition to become a Mason, he must come before
the Lodge in perfect gooil faith and most implicit sincerity. There must be no folse
suggestions in his petition, nor fraudulent, willful, or negligent concealme.nt of material facts. His petition stands as the basis of the contract between him and tho
Lodge· anil if it is false materially, wl1ether the falsehood proceed from culpable
neglig.'nce or intentional fraud, on proof of that fact the Lodge wou.ld be e_nti.tleu, if
it so desired, to rescind the contract on its part, and expel or otherwise d1sc1plme the
offending party.
In this case it cannot be doubted that the Lodge would have rejected the ap.
plicant if it had known the true facts of bis status. Can it be urge ii, then, t.hat he
can take advantage of his owu wrong and say:-" I suppressed or negligently
mistated facts which, if you had known, you would not have received me ; but now
that you have done so you must retain me." We thin!i this question must be
answered in the negativ~. We regret that the appellant has placed himself in this
position, as, from the testimony, he appears to bear a good reputation in tl~e cor~1munity, though we are apprized tllat the vrosecution dill not make that an issue m
the ease. The entire record exhibits, at least, a highly culpoble negltgence on the
part of the appellant, if not actual framlulent suppression of the trnlh ; and wo
therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, That the action of Pmgress Lodge, No. 125, in e:xpelling JonN H.
Bmrns from all tlle rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby con·
firmed.

Bro. Tnoius A. Bn.owN, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports:To the .lf.-. W.-, (Ji-and Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the following proposition from Bro. J. p.
Miller, viz:-" An Entered Apprentice, made elsewhere, petitions a Lodge for
the second and third degrees. Accompanying his petition is a permission from the
Lodge in wl1ich the first degree was conferretl, for any other Lodge to receive his
application for those other two. Can the Lodge to which Ile applies confer those
degrees without Ruhjecting the canilidate to the ordeal of the ballot ?"-have given it
due consideration, and report as follows:Sections 2 und 3, of Article III, Part III, of our Constitution, plainly state that
every application" for the degrees of l\fasonry" must be referred to a committee•
reported upon, and balloted for; and that this applies to any, as well as all, of the
degrees is perfectly obvious from the fact that our Constitution allows the Lodges
who wish so to do, to receive applications for the degrees separately. The law, and
this plain construction of it, is founded upon simple common sense. .Although a
distant Lodge may have elected a candidate to receive the three degrees, and may
have conferred one upon him, it does not at all follow that some other Lodge, within
whose jurisdiction he has recently arriveil, and to whose members he is perhaps an
utter stranger, should confer the ·remaining degrees upon him without first endeavor·
ing to ascertain bis worthiness. The permission is not a request to do the work for
the Lodge granting it, but simply authorizes some other Lo<lge, if it shall please, to
confer the remaining degree or degrees ; and it is given only because both our own
Constitution and the common law of Masonry forbid that any Lo.dge shall complete

416

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 12,

the unfinished work of another without its assent. It would be singular, indeed, if
an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft were to be con>idered entitled to receive the
remaining degrees or degree upon terms of Jess careful scrutiny than our lnwA pro·
viile for the application of a Master Mason for affiliation ; and your committee have
no hesitation in saying that a petition for any degree or degrees must be referred,
reported on, and balloted for, unless there be a dispensation from the Grand Master
in regard to the reference, which our Constitution permits.
.A.11 which is respectfully submitted.

To the M.'. W:. Grand Lodge of California:your committee to whom was referred that portion of the Address of the Grand
Master refel'ring to the alleged invasion, by a Lodge of this jurisdiction, of the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Nevada, and the general question' of jurisdictional
rights growing out of said occurrence, having considered the subject, respectfully
report:The matter is one of grave importance, involving, as it does, the peace and harmony of the Craft, and that comity which should e1•er exist between the Grand
Bodies of the Fraternity. The controversy on this subject between Maine and
England has not passed from the memory of the brethren, nor have we forgotten
the unanimity' with which the Grand f,odges of this continent rallied to the support
of our sister of Maine in the position which she then took. This Grand Lodge has
always insisted upou what it deemed its rights over profanes, citizens of this State,
and has always been prompt to accord the same. rights to others. The Report of tlie
Committee on Correspondence, submitted at this Communication, discusses the subject somewhat fully, and, in the opinion of this committee, takes the true ground ;
the only one which can be properly maintained by any Grand Lodge, and which,
while it secures its own rights in the premises, fully acknowledges the rights of
others.
Your committee express tl1eir cordial approval of the prompt action of the Grand
:Master in taking steps to purge the Grand Lodge of California of all appearance of
disregard for the jurisdictional rights of another and co-equal Grand Lodge, and
trust that no occasion will again 1uise for a like exercise of power.
.A.11 which is respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM c. BELCHER,

Bro. HENRY II. RHEES, from the special committee on Uniformity of
Work, presented the following report : To the M.·. W." Grand Lodge of California :The special committee, to whom was referred so much of the Grand Master's
Address as relates to work, to the *circular issued by him to the Lodges in regard
thereto, and to the failure of certain of the Lodges to respond, baving carefully considered the matters committed to them, report that in the pr!i/gress made toward the
attaiument of uniformity they find great cause for congrat~ation and encouragement. The plan' adopted appears to have worked well, evP,n better than the large
number of Lodges not responding to the Grand Master's circular would seem to indicate, as your committee have information tlmt, in many of the cases named, the circular was never received, and tl1ey would fain believe that such was the reason for
the failure to respond in most of the cases. But they are sorry to be compelled to
say that in some instances this has not been the reason for such lack of reply. Some
of the J,odges have wholly neglected and refused to avail themselves of the opportunity to learn the work, as adopted and made obligatory upon them by this Grand
Body; and, if the resolutions and edicts of the Grand Lodge on the snbjeet of uniformity of work are not to be a mere dead letter-if tliey were promulgated after
due deliberation, and the Lodges have had ample time to learn the work established
for this jurisdiction -then those which are contumacions should be taught that the
edicts of the Grand Lodge can not safely be treated with contempt. It would be
unjust to those Lodges which have cheerfully complied with the law, to pass by
without some measure of censure such an evidence of insubordination. The zeal
of the chief executive of the Grand Lodge in seeking to insure the obedience of th&
subordinates to the edicts in this regard, meets with our heartiest approval ; 11nd, believing that whoever may occupy that high position will temper justice with mercy,
we recommend that the rnbject be referred to the Grand Master to be elected at
this Communication, with the request that he will take such steps as, in his wisdom,
he may deem best, to enforce and render effectual the edicts passed in 1863 and 1864
in regard to uniformity of work.

Bro. lh:rnY II. HARTLEY, from the Committee on Grievances, presented the following reports : To the],[,., W.'. Grand Lodge of California:Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred the petition of THOMAS W.
MooRE, praying to be restored "to the rights and privileges of Masoery, he having
been expelled by Santa Cruz Lodge, No. 38, in the year 1861, report that they have
examined the record of the trial and conviction of the petitioner, and find that he
was expelled for an alleged attempt to defraud a Master Mason in the purchase, or
attempt to purchase, a claim of title to certain premises owned or claimed by a
Mason. While your committee are of the opinion that there was probably sufficient
in the original record to have justified the action of the Lodge, yet this is one of that
class of cases in which extreme caution should be used to avoid bringing the daily
transactions of business before our tribunals. Not regarding the original offense as
one of extreme enormity, or as having been very distinctly proven, and considering
the fact that the then Master of the petitioner's Lodge, and the chairman of the
commission who tried him, as also the present Senior Warden of said Lodge, recommend his restoration ; and also considering that the petitioner has been already
punished by an expulsion of five years, that his general conduct during his expulsion
appears to have been unobjectionable, that the members of the Lodge to w!Jich he
belonged have generally been aware of his proposed application, and that no protest
has been filed or any cause shown against it, your committee recommend the adop·
tion of the following resolution :Resolved, That THOMAS W. MOORE, heretofore expelled by Santa Cruz Lodge, No.
38, be and Ile is hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
All which is respectfully submitted.
HENRY H. HARTLEY,
JAMES L. ENGLISH,
JAMES ANDERSON,
FRANCIS WILLIAMS,
GEORGE w. CRANE,

Th the JI:. W." Grand Lodge of California :Your Committee on Grievances have necessarily, in the discharge of their
duties, had their attention called to the manner in which applications for restoration
are made to the Grand Lodge on tM part of expelled Masons. They find that such
applications are generally made ex parte and without any previous notice or information being given to the Lodge of which the expelled party was formerly a member; and, feeling convinced that this course tends to the possibility of imposition
being practiced upon the Grand Lodge, or at least that it is prevented from obtaining the fullest information in regard to the propriety of the application; and being
of the opinion that a beneficial result would follow from a previous promulgation of
the intention of the applicant to apply to the Grand Lodge for restoration, subjoin
the following resolution, and recommend that it be adopted as one of the General
Regulations :-

Resolved, That whenever it is the intention of a person, who has been expelled
from the rights and privileges of Masonry, to petition the Grand Lodge for restoration, it shall be his duty to notiFy the Lodge which expelled him of such intention,
at least sixty days before the meeting of the Grand Lodge, accompanying said notice
with a copy of his intended petition ; and before said petition shall be considered
by the Grand Lodge, proof shall be made of the giving of said notice.
All which is respectfully submitted.
HENRY H. HARTLEY,
JAMES L, ENGLISH,
JAMES ANDERSON,

Bro. WILLIAM A. DAVIES, from the special committee to whom was
referred that portion of the Grand Master's Address relative to the Ma·
sonic Board of Relief of the city of San Francisco, presented the following
report:-

To the M.'. W." Gmnd Lodge of California:Your committee. to whom was referred so much of the Grand Master's Address
as relates to the Masonic Board of Relief of the city of San Frnncisco, have had
placed in their hands, not only the report of that Board for the past year, bnt a·
detailed and voluminous statement, transcribed from its books, of its expenditures
during the whole period of its existence. A careful examination has fully satisfied
your committee of the entire correctness of that statement, which corresponds with
the annual reports presented to this Grand Lodge during the past eleven years; and,
when they consider the very large amount thus shown to have been disbursed for
charity by the Lodges of this city to those, in all cases, belonging elsewhere, not
_only does their pr.esent request for aid from. the Grand Lodge seem most reasonable,
but it is a matter of surprise that it has not been earlier presented. At this, the
great depot of the Pacific coast, the sick and destitute accumulate, not only from
all portions of our State, but from all parts of the world; and the well organized
system for their relief which has been established by our brethren of San Francisco,
and the generous and truly Masonic liberality which has ever characterized its operation, have not only been a cause for just pride by our Grand Lodge, but have been
the subject of much and frequent commern\ation by the Grand Lodges of other
States. It will be seen that the aggregate expenditure, during the existence of this
Board of Helief, has been $53,439, of which sum, $14,123 has been for the relief of
brethren of this State, or their widows or orphans; and it is to be remembered that
of this whole amount, not one dollar has been disbursed for the assiotance of members of Lodges in this city, or their families, as, in those respects, each Lodge provides
for itself, at an additional expense, perhaps nearly equaling the annual amount
bestowed upon stranger brethren.
Your committee are aware that much credit is also due to the organizations of a
similar character in the cities of Sacramento and Marysville, but as the only business
referred to them concerns the Board of Relief of San Francisco, it is of that alone
t11ey write. From the report of the present year it appears that the expenditures
have exceeded the income, (after paying the deficit of the previons yeor,) in the
sum of $1,573 55, which amount has been advanced by the members of the Board;
and, as it is certainly just that the Grand J,odge should give it such aid as its means
will permit, it is thought that a donation to that amount, which will free the Board
from de ht, will be but a proper recognition of its fair claim for assistance. Your
committee, therefore, offer the following resolution, and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That this Grand Lodge appropriate, out of any moneys in its treasury,
the sum of $1,573 55 for the aid of the Masonic Board of Helief of the City of San
Francisco, and that the Grand Secretary be instruoted to draw an order upon the
Grand Treasurer therefor.
All which is respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM A. DAYIES,
BENJAMIN AKERLY,
FREDERICK F. BARBS,
Committee.
LEONARD Goss,
CHARLES E. S'rONE,

was referred to the Committee on Finances.

MOST WORSHIPFUL Sm AND BROTHER
There are few duties belonging to the high station, so long by you adorned, and
for a season oceupied by him who now addresses you, which it is not an absolute
pleasure to discharge; but it sometimes happens that there is one which it is preeminently pleasant to fulfill. With the performance of such an one I am happy enough
this day to be intrnsted, and I only i·egret my inability so to accomplish it
to set
forth in fitting words both my own personal attachment and regard, and the sincere
and affectionate esteem of those for whom I am now deputed to speak. At the last
Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge, when you voluntarily retired from the
office of Grand Master, the following resolution was adopted:" Re.~olr:f!a, That the elective Grand Officers be appointed a committee to procure
a suitable testimonial for presentation to Past Grand l\Iaster WILI,IAM C. BELO HER, at
the next Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge, as an evidence of its just ap·
preciation of the able, zealous, and faithful manner in which .the duties of the Grand
Mastership have been performed by him during more than three years past, and of
its desire to do honor to one with whom it has so long been so happily associated.''

as

This pleasing mandate of the Grand Lodge has been obeyed, and the taste and
judgment of that Grand Officer to whom, by the others, its execution was more im·
mediately confided, have been evinced not less in this than in the many other things
which our well-deserved confidence bas heretofore committed to his care. '.l'here is
little which I can add to the exp1·ession of fraternal and grateful feeling intended to
be conveyed in the language of that resolution; and, in officially presenting to you
the fruition of that sentiment, as exhibited in tlle beautiful service of silver now
before you, I feel well assured that you will prize it as does the hr.ave soldier the
badge which distinguishes him for meritorious service in a cause of which he is
justly proud, and as an evidence that your labors are known to have increased the
prosperity of that eminently good cause in which your heart has always entered
with a full devotion.
On the principal piece of the service which I am now honored in offering to your
acceptance, you will find engraved the following words:--" To the M.·. W.-. WILLIAM
CALDWELJ, BELCIIEn, Past Grand Master, this, witll fifteen accompanying pieces of
plate, was presented by the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepter! Masons of the State
of California, at its Annual Communication in October, A. L. 5866, as an evidence
of its just appreciation of his services as its Grand ]\faster, from May, A. L. 5862, to
October, A. L. 5865 ;" and upon all the other pieces will be found more brief inscrip·
tions conveying a similar sentiment.
Words of mine can add nothing to that which here is meant; and, congratulating
you upon the exhibition of that zeal, ability, and watchful care, during your long

T;king this, with the excess last year of nearly equal amount, as a fair average

considerations:.
They are of the opinion that the existing regullltions in regard to the disposition
of the Representative Fund do not fully meet the requirements of the case, and that
the same spirit which prompted the proposition to pay the "necessary traveling
expenses" of representatives," to and from the place of the Communications,''
would suggest the propriety of allowing some such sum per diem as would defray
their other necessary expenses while in attendance thereat.
They therefore recommend that the thirteenth and fourteenth General Regulations
be so amended that the dues on account of the Representative Fund, for each mem·
ber borne upon the rolls of the several Lodges, shall be one dollar per annum, instead
of seventy-five cents, as at present; and that there shall be paid to the representative
of each Lodge, and to each appointed Grand Officer and Chairman of a Standing

Bro. THOMAS BECK, from the Committee on Finances, presented the
following report;-

•

Th fhe ]tf.•. W.-, (}rand. Lodge OJ California :Your committee, to whom was referred a resolution proposing to abolish the office
of· Grand Lecturer, and to substitute therefor five Deputy Grand Lecturers, withont salary from the Grand Lodge, have given the same due consideration, and report
as follows :• . . .
They are of the opinion that, if uniformity in the w?rk thronghout t~e Jur1sd1,ct10n
is deemed desirable, as by all well informed Masons it undoubtedly 1s, the SJstem
which is to be taught in order to secure it must have but one head-one central
eource whence shall liow all the teachings of our ritual to be disseminated among tlie
Lodges and brethren of the State. To have five independent Lectmers would be
to secure a confusion worse perhaps than that which reigned wben we had none at
all for then there was at least a dim remembrance of the work as taught years ago,
when there was, a.q now, a Grnnd Lecturer charged with that importa~t duty . . An
ill·judged economy then dispensed with the services of that officer, JUSt at a time
when his usefulness was greatest, and it soon became apparent that a great mistake
had been committed.
For years past it has been ardently desired that some system for the. dissemination
of a uniform mode of work should be again established, and in a portwn of the Address of Grand Master BELCHER, in 1863, and the report of the Committee on ,Jnris·
prudence for that year' will be found well set forth the embodiment of that general
desire. No "new " work: was sought for or thought of, as in those papers, and in all.
the legislation of the Grand Lodge upon that subject since the year 1855, when t~e
work as tben agreed upon became a regulation, that work was and bas ~e_;m considered as the Jaw of the jurisdietion. Unfortunately, however, the abolition of th!!
:Office of Grand J,ecturer left no one to teach it and continue it in r~membr~nce, ~nd.
>the natural consequences followed. Frailties of memory, irnprovmg and mvent1ve
young Masons, and immigrations from other juriscictions, soon crea~ed almost a.a
grea.t a confueion in the work of the J,odges of our State as there was m the tongues

1866.]

Grand Lodge of Cal:ifornia.

431

at the tower of Babel ; and it was for the purpose of ascertaining, examining, and
revising the ritua\ previously ordained, and of de,·ising the most efficient means for
i:s general dissemination, that the committee of 1863 was ordered by the Grand
Lodge. That committee consisted of the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master,
and three Past Masters chosen by the officer first nameil, and their action has receiv•
ed tbe continued approval of this body.
That the system has worked well, so far as time and opportunity have permitted,
is very evident. The Grand Lecturer teaches the work to all who come to him from
every portion of the State ; and to those who have remained long enough to learn,
and have actually learned the work and lectures thoroughly and completely, he issues
certificates to that effect, (if they desire it,) upon the receipt of which tl1e Grand
Master gives them appointments as D&puty Grand J,ecturers. They then go forth
among the Lodges in the several portions of the jurisdiction whence they come, and
as there is no limit, save that of qualification, to the nnrnber which maybe appointed,
there will soon be such facilities for instruction that no Lodge can have excuse for
being ignorant of, or not conforming to the ritual of the Grand Lodge. When it is
known, as it is known to the writer of this report, himself a Deputy Grand J,ecturer,
that two or three weeks-sometimBs even more-are required to become thoroughly
taught in the work, and that there have been many who sought to learn it, the office
of Grand Lecturer wiJI by no means be considered a sinecure ; and your committee
have no hesitation in saying that the salary of that officer is well and most laboriously
earned.
It is an error, therefore, to suppose that five independent Lecturers could properly
instruct, and keep instructed, the hundred and fifty Lodges of this widely spread jurisdiction. Aside from the differences and discrepancies which the fallibility of human
memory would inevitably produce·among them, it would be a physical impossibility.
It is not a visit or two to a Lodge-the conferring of two or three degrees--the "exemplification of the work" in its presence-which teaches anything of valne ; but it
is tbe assembling of its officers and drilling them for days, and nights, and weeks, if
necessary, untH they are perfectly and thoroughly conversan1 with the work, tbat is
to impart it to its members and make its initiates properly instructed Masvns. How
long a time would be required, then, even supposing every Lodge to desire !Uld be
ready for their presence, for five brethren to traverse this State and thus fully and
properly give tbem all instruction? Even with t:he twenty-five or thirty Deputies
who have thus far been appointed, besides a number of Masters and other officers
who have learned the work for their own Lodges only, perhaps not more than half
the Lodges have as yet obtained the work. But in most cases, probably, this failure
has been because there was no Deputy residing near them, and it was expensive t(\
send for one from a distance. As those officers are increased and more widely scattered throughout the State, the knowledge of the work will be more completely disseminated. It would be unwise to change a system which has plainly been beneficial thus far, and the continuance of which the evidences contained in the Grand
Master's Address, and our own observation, show to be necessary tor the complete
fruition of the hopes entertained at its establishment; and, strongly impressed witk
these views, your committee report back the resolution with the recommendation
that it be not adopted.
All which is respectfully submitted •
CHALES MARSH,
}
Wn,LIAM M. RUNDELL,

Bro. CHARLES E. IluTTON, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, pre·
sented the following report:2'b IJte M.·. W.·. Grand 'Lodge of California :Your committee have had under consideration the question submitted by Ilro.
ISAAC T. COFFIN, which is substantially as follows:"A difterence of opinion exists as to the proper construction of our fourth Ge.n·
era! Regulation, and, that its true intent may be defined, the following is submitted:
A. B. has resided in this State severaJ years. A little less than a year ago he visited
his former home in Maine, and while there received the degrees of Masonry. Upon
his return to California he proposed to visit a Lodge, but the Master refused to ad·
mit him. He afterwards offered to visit another Lodge, and was admitted. On again
• applying to visit the first-named Lodge, should the Master admit him upon the
avouchment of a brother who had sat with him in a regular Lodge? Which Master
was right-the one who refused, or the one who permitted his admission? Would it
affect the case if the applicant stated that when he left this State he had no inten·

434

Proceedings if the

[Oct. 13,

tion to return, but afterward changed his mind? Should he apply for 11-ftlllatlon, the
regulation Is sufficiently clear ; but does it deny hlm the right to visit ? "
The regulation referred to lias no application to the right of visit. That rl&ht, 10
called, is not, as is gener.ally supposed, absolute and indefeasible. The M1111ter of a
Lodge is under obligation to preserve harmony among his craftsmen. He reprifftltll
the wise Master·bnilder who laid the foundations of our speculative science, 11114 b
must see that the guards and defenses of his Lodge are of such character that ncia.•
ing be suffered to pass or repassthemthatmight tend to disturb the peace of his Wlll't•
men. To this end he must be clothed with authority to say who, ot' those bailing fro111
other Lodges, llhall visit Ills. In regard to the brother whose case is meutioned in
the question under consideration, we think the fact of his intention to remain permanently out of the State, does affect the action of the regulation. Prima faoie an
otfense may have been committed, but often an apparent wrong ceases to be rightly
so considered when the intention is taken into account. It may well occur that one,
for several years a resident of this State, may return to the home of his youth, intending to reside permanently among the associations of his earlier days; but, find·
ing that the attachments formed in the new home ar<' stronger than those severed in
the past, detormines to return there, ere they too, like the old. ones, shall have be·
come strange by long absence. If then, having in good faith intended to change his
place of residence, he become member of the Fraternity abroad, the regulation of
this State should not operate against him upon his return. While we tenaciously adhere to and insist upon our jurisdictional rights, we should not enforce the regula·
tion refe1·red to, unless the violation of those rights is clear and pointed. Nothing is
to be gained by a too strenuous and rigid interpretation of the law.
We conclude, then, that if the brother's purpose in going to the Eastern States
was to reside permanently and become a citizen, his simple change of purpose and
return to this State within some short time, will not of itself bring him within the
regulation of this Grand Lodge. We further conclud~ that, as the regulation does
not apply to the matter of visit, and as the llfaster has control thereof, both Masters,
the one who refused, and the one who permitted the visit, were within the purview of
their powers.
All which is respectfully submitted.
